The area now known as West Virginia was a favorite hunting ground of numerous Native American peoples before the arrival of [European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_ethnic_groups "European ethnic groups") settlers. Many ancient earthen mounds constructed by various [mound builder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound_builder_(people) "Mound builder (people)") cultures survive, especially in the areas of [Moundsville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moundsville,_West_Virginia "Moundsville, West Virginia"), [South Charleston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Charleston,_West_Virginia "South Charleston, West Virginia"), and [Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romney,_West_Virginia "Romney, West Virginia"). The artifacts uncovered in these give evidence of a village society having a tribal trade system culture that practiced the [cold working](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_working "Cold working") of copper to a limited extent. As of 2009[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit), over 12,500 archaeological sites have been documented in West Virginia.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-2)

[Paleo-Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleo-Indian "Paleo-Indian") culture appears by 10,500 BC in West Virginia passing along the major river valleys and ridge-line gap watersheds. Following are the traditional [Archaic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaic_period_in_the_Americas "Archaic period in the Americas") sub-periods; Early (8000–6000 BC), Middle (6000–4000 BC), and Late (4000–1000 BC).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-3) Within the greater region of and neighboring the Mountain State, the Riverton Tradition includes Maple Creek Phase. Also are the Buffalo Phase, Transitional Archaic Phase, Transitional Period Culture and Central Ohio Valley Archaic Phase. Also within the region is the Laurentian Archaic Tradition, which includes Brewerton Phase, Feeley Phase, Dunlop Phase, McKibben Phase, Genesee Phase, Stringtown/Satchel Phase, Satchel Phase and Lamoka/Dustin Phase.

The [Adena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adena_culture "Adena culture") provided the greatest cultural influence in the state. For practical purposes the Adena is Early [Woodland period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodland_period "Woodland period") according to [West Virginia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia_University "West Virginia University")'s Dr. Edward V. McMichael,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-4) also among the 1963 [Geological Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geological_Survey "Geological Survey"). Middle and Late Woodland people include Middle Woodland Watson pottery people, Late Woodland Wood Phase, Late Hopewell at Romney, Montana (late Woodland AD 500–1000), Wilhelm culture (Late Middle Woodland, c. AD 1~500), Armstrong (Late Middle Woodland, c. AD 1~500), Buck Garden (Late Woodland AD 500–1200), Childers Phase (Late Middle Woodland c. 400 AD), and Parkline Phase (Late Woodland AD 750~1000). Adena villages can be characterized as rather large compared to Late Prehistoric tribes.

The Adena Indians used ceremonial pipes that were exceptional works of art. They lived in round (double post method) wicker sided and bark sheet roofed houses.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-5) Little is known about the housing of Paleo-Indian and Archaic periods, but Woodland Indians lived in wigwams. They grew sunflowers, tubers, gourds, squash and several seeds such as lambsquarter, may grass, sumpweed, smartweed and little barley cereals. In the Fort Ancient period, Indians lived in much larger poled rectangular shaped houses with walls hide covered.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-6) They were farmers who cultivated large fields around their villages, concentrating on corn, [beans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bean "Bean"), [tubers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuber "Tuber"), [sunflowers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunflower "Sunflower"), [gourds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gourd "Gourd") and many types of [squash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squash_(plant) "Squash (plant)") including the pumpkin. They also raised domestic turkeys and kept dogs as pets. Their neighbors in the northerly of the state, the Monongahela houses were generally circular in shape often with nook or storage appendage. Their living characteristics were more of a heritage from the Woodland Indians.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-7)

The Late Prehistoric (c. AD 950–1650) phases of the Fort Ancient Tradition include Feurt Phase, Blennerhassett Phase, Bluestone Phase, Clover Complex followed by the Orchard Phase (c. AD 1550–1650) with a Late Proto-historic arrival of a Lizard Cult from the [Southeastern Ceremonial Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Ceremonial_Complex "Southeastern Ceremonial Complex"). Contemporaneously to Fort Ancient Tradition southerly of the state, the _sister culture_ called Monongahela is found on the northerly of the Mountain State stemming from the Drew Tradition.

Historically recorded names of tribes with regards to what is now West Virginia include Calicua, Mohetan, Moneton, Monecaga, Monahan, Tomahitan, Kanawha, Shattara, Shenandoah, Lenape, Ouabano, Guyan, Guyandotte, Little Mingo, Tionontatecaga & Shawnee. Archaeology has shown that the area was mostly divided up between Susquehannocks, Saponi-Tutelo, Manahoac, Fort Ancients & the Monongahela Culture when whites arrived. Among Early Scots-Irish and German settlers, however, Cherokee came to be a catch all term for all Native people and that is a term that pops up most often in the historical record.

A few of these are solvable. Shattara is a Yuchi word, traceable back to a village recorded in Yuchi territory, so it seems they may have split off from the Yuchi when the Coosa Chiefdom (original union of Yuchi and Cherokee peoples in Southern Appalachia) dissolved.

Tionontatecaga is the exact same name used for a small Iroquoian Nation originally from western New York, who had lived between the Iroquois, Neutral Nation and Erie otherwise called the Wenro, Petun or Tobacco. They were the first tribe attacked at the outset of the Beaver Wars in the 1630s and are known to have relocated to the shores of Lake Huron. The placement of this tribe on maps overlaps the Kanawha River and places the Guyandotte frequented, who were also an Iroquoian people known in the area after the Beaver Wars and are often confused with the Wyandot of northern Ohio. Likely, either the Wenro split in the 1630s, with some moving to Canada and others migrating South, or some took refuge among the Erie following the second defeat by the Iroquois and those moved further south after the Erie were defeated in the 1650s, or the Iroquois purposely stationed captured Petun to hold this area for them in a forgotten chapter of the Beaver Wars.

Calicua first appears in DeSoto's accounts of his travels. Given many of the cities he visited collapsed between his visit and colonization of the east coast, many were never quite sure where to place many of the tribes he says he encountered, leading to this term being plastered generally over the area where the Fort Ancients and Monongahela culture were located on maps for many years. It is now believed that this was a village in what is now southern Missouri. Ergo, this tribe may have not even existed in the first place.

Ouabano is not the name of a tribe, but a common Algonquian term for a shaman. It's possible it's even confusing a name of an actual group of Natives associated with the Mohicans that settled in Central Pennsylvania following the Revolutionary War called the Wappinger, until their removal to Wisconsin after 1830, but these Mohicans never formally settled in West Virginia. It usually comes up in claims of Native American Heritage among locals.

Shenandoah were never encountered by whites in any historical account, but were well associated with the Shenandoah Valley and are brought up in the historical record twice. Archaeology shows a war against the occupants of the valley from the north just before the arrival of whites. One account claims the Shenandoah were at war with the Catawba and Tutelo, before being wiped out. All of this comes from the period of the Beaver Wars. What we do know is that Susquehannocks have been shown to have held parts of West Virginia north of the Potomac and east of the Monongahela when whites arrived on the continent. They became involved in the Beaver Wars and eventually lost to the Irpquois and were absorbed by them in the 1680s. Afterwards, the Iroquois went to war with the Manahoac and Saponi, most of whom fled South to live with the Catawba. Along with some allies from "across the mountains" before trying to return in 1701. Several attempts were made by whites to settle West Virginia in the late 1600s, but it was politically argued that the area belonged to the Iroquois. The first settlers were allowed to move in immediately after the Iroquois give up ownership, which seems to coincide with the disappearance of the Shenandoah. The likely conclusion is that the Shenandoah were a group of Susquehannock who were holding the area for the Iroquois and the main front in their war against the Saponi.

Beyond that, the area was mostly known for Lenape, Guyandotte and Shawnee when whites first began moving in. It is believed the Guyandotte merged with the Senecas of Ohio around the 1750s. The Shawnee quickly began abandoning most of West Virginia upon arrival of white settlers and were mostly seen in the southern portions of the state and across the river, in Ohio. They largely left West Virginia altogether following Dunmore's War and most of them were forced to leave the entire region after the Shawnee War, with the last groups relocated West after 1830. A large group of Lenape moved in to the area between the Potomac River in Maryland and the Mahoning River in Ohio, as well as throughout Southern and Central Ohio, after they lost too much land to the Walking Purchase in 1690. The English crown forced the easternmost Lenape to act as a tribe of Iroquois and have an Iroquoian style of government, with chiefs approved by the Iroquois government. Towards the end of the French-Indian Wars, Lenape from Ohio were attacking settlers in West Virginia. Afterwards predicting that this would lead to another forced removal, the eastern Lenape chief, Tamaqua (King Beaver), decided to voluntarily begin relocating his people West in the 1740s-50s. He ended up being correct, with a decree from the royal crown stripping the land between the Potomac and Mahoning Rivers from the Lenape in the 1760s. Most of these Lenape relocated into what is now Tuscarawas and Holmes Counties in Ohio, however the Tuscarawas communities were devastated during the Revolutionary War and the Holmes County settlement followed suit in the early 1800s from a posse of white settlers led by a disgruntled former chief. Afterwards, these eastern Lenape seem to have fully collapsed into the other Lenape communities in central Ohio.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-8)

Within the Mountain State these tribal villages can be characterized as rather small and scattered as they moved about the _old fields_ every couple of generations. Many would join other tribes and remove to the midwest regions as settlers arrived in the state. Although, there were those who would acculturate within the historic as sometimes called _Fireside Cabin_ culture. Some are early historic documented seeking protection closer, moving to the easterly colonial trade towns. And later, other small splintered clans were attracted to, among others, [James Le Tort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Le_Tort "James Le Tort"), Charles Poke and John Van Metre trading houses within the state. This historic period changed the way of living extends from a little before the 18th century Virginia and Pennsylvania region [North American fur trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_fur_trade "North American fur trade") beginning on the Eastern Panhandle of the state.

## European exploration and settlement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: European exploration and settlement")]

Main articles: [Colony of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_Virginia "Colony of Virginia"), [French and Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_and_Indian_War "French and Indian War"), [Treaty of Paris (1763)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Paris_(1763) "Treaty of Paris (1763)"), and [Indian Reserve (1763)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Reserve_(1763) "Indian Reserve (1763)")

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/Col._Thomas_Lee_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Col._Thomas_Lee_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Col._Thomas_Lee_(cropped).jpg)

[Thomas Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Lee_(Virginia_colonist) "Thomas Lee (Virginia colonist)"), the first manager of the [Ohio Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Company "Ohio Company") of Virginia

In 1671 General [Abraham Wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Wood "Abraham Wood"), at the direction of Royal Governor [William Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Berkeley_(governor) "William Berkeley (governor)") of the [Virginia Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Colony "Virginia Colony"), sent the party of Thomas Batts and Robert Fallum into the West Virginia area. During this expedition the pair followed a tributary of the Kanawha River they named [Woods River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_River_(Kanawha_River) "New River (Kanawha River)") for their sponsor, and discovered [Kanawha Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanawha_Falls "Kanawha Falls"). Their journey continued northward (upriver) or westward over land, and there is ambiguity where they went.

On July 13, 1709, Louis Michel, George Ritter, and Baron [Christoph von Graffenried](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christoph_von_Graffenried "Christoph von Graffenried") petitioned the King of England for a land grant in the [Harpers Ferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpers_Ferry,_West_Virginia "Harpers Ferry, West Virginia"), [Shepherdstown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shepherdstown,_West_Virginia "Shepherdstown, West Virginia") area, [Jefferson County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_County,_West_Virginia "Jefferson County, West Virginia"), to establish a [Swiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swiss_people "Swiss people") colony. Neither the land grant or the Swiss colony ever materialized.

Lt. Governor [Alexander Spotswood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Spotswood "Alexander Spotswood") is sometimes credited with taking his 1716 "[Knights of the Golden Horseshoe Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knights_of_the_Golden_Horseshoe_Expedition "Knights of the Golden Horseshoe Expedition")" into what is now [Pendleton County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pendleton_County,_West_Virginia "Pendleton County, West Virginia"), although according to contemporary accounts, Spotswood's trail went no farther west than [Harrisonburg, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrisonburg,_Virginia "Harrisonburg, Virginia"). The Treaty of Albany, 1722, designated the [Blue Ridge Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Ridge_Mountains "Blue Ridge Mountains") as the western boundary of white settlement,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-wvculture.org-9) and recognized [Iroquois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iroquois "Iroquois") rights on the west side of the ridge, including all of West Virginia. Though the Iroquois made little effort to settle the region themselves, they made war throughout the area with their enemies, following the Great Indian Warpaths through the region and, some time between 1725 and 1750, contracted a large group of the Saponi-Tutelo warriors the Iroquois had living on the Susquehanna River in Pennsylvania to fight alongside them in the region.

Other tribes, notably the [Shawnee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawnee "Shawnee") and [Cherokee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee "Cherokee"), used the resources of the region as well. Soon after this, white settlers began moving into the [Greater Shenandoah-Potomac Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shenandoah_Valley "Shenandoah Valley") making up the entire eastern portion of the state. They found it largely unoccupied, apart from [Tuscaroras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuscarora_people "Tuscarora people") who had lately moved into the area around [Martinsburg, WV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martinsburg,_WV "Martinsburg, WV"), some Shawnee villages in the region around [Moorefield, WV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorefield,_WV "Moorefield, WV") and [Winchester, VA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester,_VA "Winchester, VA"), and frequent passing bands of "Northern Indians" ([Lenape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenape "Lenape") from the Delaware Valley) and "Southern Indians" ([Catawba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catawba_(tribe) "Catawba (tribe)") from South Carolina) who were engaged in a bitter long-distance war, using the Valley as a battleground.

John Van Metre, an Indian trader, penetrated into the northern portion of West Virginia in 1725. Also in 1725, _Pearsall's Flats_ in the [South Branch Potomac River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Branch_Potomac_River "South Branch Potomac River") valley, present-day [Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romney,_West_Virginia "Romney, West Virginia"), was settled, and later became the site of the [French and Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_and_Indian_War "French and Indian War") stockade, [Fort Pearsall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Pearsall "Fort Pearsall"). [Morgan ap Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_Morgan "Morgan Morgan"), a Welshman, built a cabin near present-day [Bunker Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunker_Hill,_West_Virginia "Bunker Hill, West Virginia") in [Berkeley County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkeley_County,_West_Virginia "Berkeley County, West Virginia") in 1727. The same year German settlers from [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania") founded _New Mecklenburg_, the present [Shepherdstown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shepherdstown,_West_Virginia "Shepherdstown, West Virginia"), on the [Potomac River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potomac_River "Potomac River"), and others soon followed.

Orange County, [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia") was formed in 1734. It included all areas west of the [Blue Ridge Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Ridge_Mountains "Blue Ridge Mountains"), constituting all of present West Virginia. However, in 1736 the Iroquois Six Nations protested Virginia's colonization beyond the demarcated Blue Ridge, and a skirmish was fought in 1743. The Iroquois were on the point of threatening all-out war against the Virginia Colony over the "Cohongoruton lands", which would have been destructive and devastating, when Governor Gooch bought out their claim for 400 pounds at the [Treaty of Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Lancaster "Treaty of Lancaster") (1744).

In 1661 King [Charles II of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") had granted a company of gentlemen the land between the Potomac and [Rappahannock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rappahannock_River "Rappahannock River") rivers, known as the [Northern Neck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Neck "Northern Neck"). The grant eventually came into the possession of [Thomas Fairfax, 6th Lord Fairfax of Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Fairfax,_6th_Lord_Fairfax_of_Cameron "Thomas Fairfax, 6th Lord Fairfax of Cameron") and in 1746 [a stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax_Stone "Fairfax Stone") was erected at the source of the [North Branch Potomac River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Branch_Potomac_River "North Branch Potomac River") to mark the western limit of the grant. A considerable part of this land was surveyed by [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington"), especially the [South Branch Potomac River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Branch_Potomac_River "South Branch Potomac River") valley between 1748 and 1751. The diary kept by Washington indicates that there were already many squatters, largely of German origin, along the South Branch. [Christopher Gist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Gist "Christopher Gist"), a surveyor for the first [Ohio Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Company "Ohio Company"), which was composed chiefly of Virginians, explored the country along the [Ohio River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River") north of the mouth of the [Kanawha River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanawha_River "Kanawha River") in 1751 and 1752. The company sought to have a fourteenth colony established with the name _[Vandalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandalia\_(colony) "Vandalia (colony)")_.

### Early river traffic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early river traffic")]

Further information: [Waterways of West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterways_of_West_Virginia "Waterways of West Virginia")

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/Kitfry-1-.jpg/250px-Kitfry-1-.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kitfry-1-.jpg)

1751 [Fry-Jefferson map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fry-Jefferson_map "Fry-Jefferson map") showing early ferries and established colonial borders before the [French And Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_And_Indian_War "French And Indian War")

By 1739 Thomas Shepherd had constructed a flour mill powered by water from the Town Run or the Falling Springs Branch of the [Potomac River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potomac_River "Potomac River") in present-day Shepherdstown.

In October 1748 the [Virginia General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_General_Assembly "Virginia General Assembly") passed an act establishing a ferry across the [Potomac River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potomac_River "Potomac River") from the landing of Evan Watkin near the mouth of [Conococheague Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conococheague_Creek "Conococheague Creek") in present-day [Berkeley County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkeley_County,_West_Virginia "Berkeley County, West Virginia") to the property of Edmund Wade in [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland"). In March 1761, Robert Harper obtained a [permit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/License "License") to operate a ferry across the [Shenandoah River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shenandoah_River "Shenandoah River") at present-day Harpers Ferry, Jefferson County.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-wvculture.org-9) The two ferry crossings became the earliest locations of government authorized civilian commercial crafts on what would become a part of the West Virginia Waterways.

During the late 17th and early 18th centuries a growing demand for [beaver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaver "Beaver") sent trappers up and down the Kanawha region's tributary creeks by [canoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canoe "Canoe") and [raft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft "Raft"). Trading posts were established at the confluence of the Ohio and Kanawha Rivers at [Point Pleasant, West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia "Point Pleasant, West Virginia") where, in the mid-1780s, [Daniel Boone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Boone "Daniel Boone") resided for several years. Likewise, [St. Albans, West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Albans,_West_Virginia "St. Albans, West Virginia"), at the confluence of the Kanawha and Coal Rivers, became a point of trade.

In the late 18th century the steel trap increased efficiency, and beaver became scarce. A shift to exporting the state's other natural resources began. Kanawha salt production followed by coal and timber could be seen on the waterways. A number of riverside locations were used for early [Industrial Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution") production. [Keelboats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keelboats "Keelboats") were built in the Kanawha region in Leon, Ravenswood Murraysville, and Little Kanawha River. 19th century steamboats were built and repaired in Wheeling, Parkersburg, Point Pleasant and Mason City. Wooden coal barges were built on the Monongahela River near Morgantown, as well as along [Coal River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_River_(West_Virginia) "Coal River (West Virginia)") and [Elk River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elk_River_(West_Virginia) "Elk River (West Virginia)").

The logging industry furthered the river shipping industry. A horse-drawn logging "tram" with a special block and tackle for hill-side harvesting was brought into use, allowing expansion of Crooked Creek and the opening of a wooden barrel plant at the creek's mouth. In the 1880s, this tram and other steam machinery were used for collecting timber used as railroad ties in the railway construction along the Kanawha river. Railroad spurs were built throughout West Virginia, connecting mines to the riverboats, barges and coal-tipples.

## Trans-Allegheny Virginia, 1768–1788

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Trans-Allegheny Virginia, 1768–1788")]

Further information: [Vandalia (colony)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandalia_(colony) "Vandalia (colony)") and [Westsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westsylvania "Westsylvania")

Further information: [History of slavery in West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_slavery_in_West_Virginia "History of slavery in West Virginia")

Many settlers crossed the mountains after 1750, though they were hindered by Native American resistance. The 1744 Treaty of Lancaster had left ambiguous whether the Iroquois had sold only as far as the [Alleghenies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_Mountains "Allegheny Mountains"), or all their claim south of the Ohio, including the rest of modern West Virginia. At the convening of the [1752 Treaty of Logstown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logstown#Treaty_of_Logstown,_1752 "Logstown"), they acknowledged the right of English settlements south of the Ohio, but the Cherokee and Shawnee claims still remained. During the [French and Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_and_Indian_War "French and Indian War") (1754–1763), the scattered settlements were almost destroyed. The [Proclamation of 1763](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_1763 "Proclamation of 1763") again confirmed all land beyond the Alleghenies as Indian Territory, but the Iroquois finally relinquished their claims south of the Ohio to Britain at the [Treaty of Fort Stanwix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Fort_Stanwix "Treaty of Fort Stanwix") in 1768. Most of the Cherokee claim within West Virginia, the southwestern part of the state, was sold to Virginia in 1770 by the [Treaty of Lochaber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Lochaber "Treaty of Lochaber"). Most early settlement was wildcat, with specious ("tomahawk") claims, and without organized governments.

Sustained settlement started with the creation of [Fincastle County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fincastle_County "Fincastle County"), Virginia in 1772, representing trans-Allegheny Virginia, encompassing most of West Virginia, all of Kentucky, and part of the "tail" of today's Virginia. In 1774, the Crown Governor of Virginia, [John Murray, 4th Earl of Dunmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Murray,_4th_Earl_of_Dunmore "John Murray, 4th Earl of Dunmore"), led a force over the mountains, and a body of militia under [Colonel Andrew Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonel_Andrew_Lewis "Colonel Andrew Lewis") dealt the [Shawnee Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawnee_Indians "Shawnee Indians") under [Cornstalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornstalk_(Shawnee_leader) "Cornstalk (Shawnee leader)") a crushing blow at the junction of the Kanawha and Ohio rivers, in the [Battle of Point Pleasant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant "Battle of Point Pleasant"). Following this conflict, known as [Dunmore's War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunmore's_War "Dunmore's War"), the Shawnee and [Mingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingo "Mingo") ceded their rights south of the Ohio, that is, to West Virginia and Kentucky.

[Fort Henry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Henry_(West_Virginia) "Fort Henry (West Virginia)") in present-day [Wheeling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheeling,_West_Virginia "Wheeling, West Virginia") played an important role in the [Western theater of the American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_theater_of_the_American_Revolutionary_War "Western theater of the American Revolutionary War"). British-allied Native tribes [besieged the American militia there in 1777](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Fort_Henry_(1777) "Siege of Fort Henry (1777)") and again in [1782](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Fort_Henry_(1782) "Siege of Fort Henry (1782)"). The battles ended in American victory and boosted morale with the heroic tale of [McColloch's Leap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McColloch's_Leap "McColloch's Leap").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-10) Renegade Cherokee chief [Dragging Canoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragging_Canoe "Dragging Canoe") continued to dispute the settlers' advance, fighting the [Cherokee–American wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee%E2%80%93American_wars "Cherokee–American wars") (1776–1794) until after the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"). During the war, the settlers in western Virginia were generally active patriots and many served in the [Continental Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Army "Continental Army").

## 1789 to 1861

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1789 to 1861")]

Social conditions in western Virginia were entirely unlike those in the eastern portion of the state. The population was not homogeneous, as a considerable part of the immigration came by way of Pennsylvania and included Germans, Protestant [Scots-Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scots-Irish_American "Scots-Irish American"), and settlers from the states farther north. Counties in the east and south were settled mostly by eastern Virginians. During the American Revolution, the movement to create a state west of the Alleghenies was revived and a petition for the establishment of "[Westsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westsylvania "Westsylvania")" was presented to Congress, on the grounds that the mountains presented an almost impassable barrier to the east. The rugged nature of the country made slavery unprofitable, and time only increased the social, political, economic, and cultural differences (see [Tuckahoes and Cohees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuckahoes_and_Cohees "Tuckahoes and Cohees")) between the two sections of Virginia.

In 1829 a constitutional convention met in Richmond to consider reforms to Virginia's outdated constitution. [Philip Doddridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Doddridge_(Virginia_politician) "Philip Doddridge (Virginia politician)") of Brooke County championed the cause of western Virginians who sought a more democratic frame of government.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-13) However, western reforms were rejected by leaders from east of the Alleghenies who "clung to political power in an effort to preserve their plantation lifestyles dependent on enslaving blacks."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-14) Virginia leaders maintained a property qualification for [suffrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffrage "Suffrage") effectively disenfranchising poorer farmers in the west, whose families did much of the farm work themselves. In addition, the [Virginia Constitutional Convention of 1829–1830](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Constitutional_Convention_of_1829%E2%80%931830 "Virginia Constitutional Convention of 1829–1830") gave the slave-owning counties the benefit of three-fifths of their slave population in apportioning representation in the [Virginia Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Assembly "Virginia Assembly"). As a result, every county west of the Alleghenies except one voted to reject the constitution, which nevertheless passed because of eastern support. Failure of the eastern planter elite to make constitutional reforms exacerbated existing east–west sectionalism in Virginia and contributed to Virginia's later split.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-15)

The [Virginia Constitutional Convention of 1850](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Constitutional_Convention_of_1850 "Virginia Constitutional Convention of 1850")–51, the Reform Convention, addressed a number of issues important to western Virginians. It extended the vote to all white males 21 years or older. The governor, lieutenant-governor, the judiciary, sheriffs, and other county officers were to be elected by public vote. The composition of the General Assembly was changed. Representation in the House of Delegates was apportioned on the basis of the census of 1850, counting whites only. The Senate representation was arbitrarily fixed at 50 seats, with the west receiving twenty, and the east thirty senators. This was made acceptable to the west by a provision that required the General Assembly to reapportion representation on the basis of white population in 1865, or else put the matter to a public referendum. But the east also gave itself a tax advantage in requiring a property tax at true and actual value, except for slaves. Slaves under the age of 12 years were not taxed and slaves over that age were taxed at only $300, a fraction of their true value. Small farmers, however, had all their assets, animals, and land taxed at full value. Despite this tax and the lack of [internal improvements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_improvements "Internal improvements") in the west, the vote was 75,748 for and 11,063 against the new Constitution. Most of the opposition came from delegates from eastern counties, who did not like the compromises made for the west.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-16)

For the western areas, problems included the long inconvenient distance from the state seat of government in [Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond,_Virginia "Richmond, Virginia") and the difference of common economic interests resultant from the tobacco and food crops farming, fishing, and coastal shipping to the east of the [Eastern Continental Divide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Continental_Divide "Eastern Continental Divide") (waters which drain to the Atlantic Ocean) along the Allegheny Mountains, and the interests of the western portion which drained to the [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River") and [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River") rivers and the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico").

The western area focused its commerce on neighbors to the west, and many citizens felt that the more populous eastern areas were too dominant in the [Virginia General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_General_Assembly "Virginia General Assembly") and insensitive to their needs. Major crises in the Virginia state government over these differences were averted on more than one occasion during the period before the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), but the underlying problems were fundamental and never well resolved. Given these differences, many in the west had long contemplated a separate state. In particular, men such as lawyer [Francis H. Pierpont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_H._Pierpont "Francis H. Pierpont") from Fairmont, had long chafed under the political domination of the Tidewater and Piedmont slave-holders. In addition to differences over the abolition of slavery, he and allies felt the Virginia government ignored and refused to spend funds on needed internal improvements in the west, such as turnpikes and railroads.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-17)

### John Brown at Harpers Ferry, 1859

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: John Brown at Harpers Ferry, 1859")]

Main article: [John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Brown's_raid_on_Harpers_Ferry "John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry")

[John Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Brown_(abolitionist) "John Brown (abolitionist)") (1800–1859), an abolitionist who saw slavery as a sin against God, led a highly aggressive and violent anti-slavery movement in Kansas (see [Bleeding Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleeding_Kansas "Bleeding Kansas")). He next planned to strike a decisive blow against Southern slavery, creating a massive "underground railroad"–type project, in the central and southern [Appalachian Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Mountains "Appalachian Mountains"), that would assist the enslaved in running away and becoming free. He had secret funding from the abolitionists in Massachusetts. With only 21 followers, in October 1859 [he took hostages and freed slaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Brown's_raid_on_Harpers_Ferry "John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry") in [Harpers Ferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpers_Ferry "Harpers Ferry"), in what is now West Virginia. Locals forced him to take refuge in the Armory firehouse, later called "[John Brown's Fort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Brown's_Fort "John Brown's Fort")"; a unit of [U.S. Marines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Marines "U.S. Marines") led by [Robert E. Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Lee "Robert E. Lee") stormed the firehouse and took Brown prisoner, almost killing him. [Brown was quickly convicted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_v._John_Brown "Virginia v. John Brown") of treason against the [Commonwealth of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Virginia "Commonwealth of Virginia"), murder, and fomenting a slave insurrection, and was hanged on December 2. Six followers were also tried, convicted, and executed. The episode enraged the pro-slavery South, which feared it portended more abolitionist violence against them.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-18)

## Civil War and split

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Civil War and split")]

Main articles: [Wheeling Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheeling_Convention "Wheeling Convention"), [State of Kanawha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Kanawha "State of Kanawha"), [Admission to the Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admission_to_the_Union "Admission to the Union"), [List of U.S. states by date of admission to the Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_by_date_of_admission_to_the_Union "List of U.S. states by date of admission to the Union"), and [West Virginia in the American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia_in_the_American_Civil_War "West Virginia in the American Civil War")

In 1861, as Virginia seceded from the United States and joined the [Confederate States of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_of_America "Confederate States of America"), the stage was set for the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") (1861–1865). Virginia was a main theatre of warfare from first to last. Union military forces controlled the western counties of Virginia. Local politicians now set up a new government recognized by Congress as the true statewide government of Virginia. The new state government authorized the formation of a separate state of West Virginia and it was recognized by President Lincoln and Congress.

### Separation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Separation")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/JCarlile.jpg/250px-JCarlile.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:JCarlile.jpg)

[John S. Carlile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_S._Carlile "John S. Carlile"), a leader during the First [Wheeling Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheeling_Convention "Wheeling Convention")

On April 17, 1861, the Richmond convention voted on the Ordinance of Secession. Of the 49 delegates from the future state of West Virginia, 17 voted in favor, and 30 voted against, and two abstained.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-20) Almost immediately after the adoption of the ordinance, a mass meeting at [Clarksburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarksburg,_West_Virginia "Clarksburg, West Virginia") recommended that each county in northwestern Virginia send delegates to a convention to meet in [Wheeling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheeling,_West_Virginia "Wheeling, West Virginia") on May 13, 1861.

When the First [Wheeling Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheeling_Convention "Wheeling Convention") met, 425 delegates from 25 counties were present, but a division of sentiment soon arose. Some delegates favored the immediate formation of a new state, while others argued that, as Virginia's secession had not yet been ratified or become effective, such action would constitute revolution against the United States.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-21) It was decided that if the ordinance was adopted (of which there was little doubt) another convention including the members-elect of the legislature should meet at Wheeling in June 1861.

In a referendum on May 23, 1861, secession was ratified by a large majority in the state as a whole. But in the western counties that would form the state of West Virginia, the vote was approximately 34,677 against and 19,121 for ratification of the Ordinance of Secession.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Wvmapagain.png/250px-Wvmapagain.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wvmapagain.png)

Counties (in blue) approving Virginia's secession from the U.S. in order to join the Confederacy.

The Second Wheeling Convention met as agreed on June 11, 1861, and adopted "A Declaration of the People of Virginia". This document, drafted by former state senator [John S. Carlile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_S._Carlile "John S. Carlile"), declared that the [Virginia Declaration of Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Declaration_of_Rights "Virginia Declaration of Rights") required any substantial change in the nature or form of the state government to be approved by the people. Therefore, since the Secession Convention had been called by the legislature and not the people, all its acts were illegal. It further declared the pro-secession government in Richmond void and called for a reorganization of the state government, taking the line that all who adhered to the Ordinance of Secession had effectively vacated their offices. The convention passed an act for the reorganization of the government on June 19, 1861. On the following day, the convention chose [Francis H. Pierpont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_H._Pierpont "Francis H. Pierpont") as governor of the "[Restored Government of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restored_Government_of_Virginia "Restored Government of Virginia")", elected other officers, and adjourned. The legislature of the Restored Government was composed of members from the western counties who had been elected on May 23, 1861, and some senators who had been elected in 1859. It met at Wheeling on July 1, 1861, filled the remainder of the state offices, completed the reorganization of the state government, and elected two United States senators who were quickly seated in Washington. There were, therefore, two governments claiming to represent all of Virginia, one owing allegiance to the United States and one to the Confederacy.

Even before the American Civil War, some people in northwest Virginia had desired to break away from Virginia to form a new state. However, the federal Constitution did not allow a new state unless the old state gave its consent. Soon after the Union government declared that the Restored Government was the legitimate government of the Commonwealth, the Restored Government asserted its authority to give such approval. It authorized the creation of the [State of Kanawha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Kanawha "State of Kanawha"), consisting of most of the counties that now comprise West Virginia. A little over one month later, Kanawha was renamed West Virginia. The Wheeling Convention, which had taken a recess until August 6, 1861, reassembled on August 20, 1861, and called for a popular vote on the formation of a new state and for a convention to frame a constitution if the vote should be favorable.

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/WVIndependenceHall.jpg/250px-WVIndependenceHall.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WVIndependenceHall.jpg)

[West Virginia Independence Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia_Independence_Hall "West Virginia Independence Hall"), site of the [Wheeling Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheeling_Convention "Wheeling Convention")

In the election held on October 24, 1861, 18,408 votes were cast for the new state and only 781 against. At this time, West Virginia had nearly 70,000 qualified voters, and the May 23, 1861 vote to secede had drawn nearly 54,000 voters.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-22) However, most of the pro-Confederate elements no longer considered themselves citizens of the United States; they saw themselves as citizens of another country (the Confederacy) and did not vote in elections sponsored by the United States. Votes from the secessionist counties in the October 24 vote on statehood were mostly cast by refugees in the area around Wheeling, not in the counties themselves.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-23) In secessionist counties where a poll was conducted it was by military intervention. Even in some counties that had voted against secession, such as Wayne and Cabell, it was necessary to send in Union soldiers.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-24)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/October_24%2C_1861_county_vote_for_West_Virginia_statehood.jpg/250px-October_24%2C_1861_county_vote_for_West_Virginia_statehood.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:October_24,_1861_county_vote_for_West_Virginia_statehood.jpg)

Turnout by county in the October 24, 1861, West Virginia statehood vote

Returns from some counties were as low as 5%, e.g. Raleigh County 32–0 in favor of statehood, Clay 76–0, Braxton 22–0, and some gave no returns at all. The Constitutional Convention began on November 26, 1861, and finished its work on February 18, 1862. The instrument was ratified on April 11, 1862, with 18,162 votes for and 514 against.

The composition of all three Wheeling Conventions, the May (First) Convention, the June (Second) Convention, and the Constitutional Convention, was of an irregular nature. The members of the May Convention were chosen by groups of Unionists, mostly in the far Northwestern counties. Over one-third came from the counties around the northern panhandle.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-25) The May Convention resolved to meet again in June 1861 should the Ordinance of Secession be ratified by public poll on May 23, 1861, which was the case. The June 1861 convention consisted of 104 members, 35 of which were members of the General Assembly in Richmond, some elected in the May 23 vote, and some hold-over State Senators. Arthur Laidley, elected to the General Assembly from Cabell County, attended the June Convention but refused to take part.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-26) The other delegates to the June Convention were "chosen even more irregularly-some in mass meetings, others by county committee, and still others were seemingly self-appointed".[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-27) It was this June Convention which drafted the statehood resolution. The Constitutional Convention met in November 1861, and consisted of 61 members. Its composition was just as irregular. A delegate representing Logan County was accepted as a member of this body, though he did not live in Logan County, and his "credentials consisted of a petition signed by fifteen persons representing six families".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-28) The large number of Northerners in this convention caused great distrust over the new Constitution during Reconstruction years. In 1872, under the leadership of [Samuel Price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Price "Samuel Price"), former Lt. Governor of Virginia, the Wheeling constitution was discarded, and an entirely new one was written along ante-bellum principles.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-29)

At first the Wheeling politicians controlled only a small part of West Virginia. However, federal forces soon drove the Confederates out of most of West Virginia.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-30)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Harper%27s_Ferry_seen_from_Maryland_side_of_Potomac_River.jpg/250px-Harper%27s_Ferry_seen_from_Maryland_side_of_Potomac_River.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harper's_Ferry_seen_from_Maryland_side_of_Potomac_River.jpg)

[Harpers Ferry, West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpers_Ferry,_West_Virginia "Harpers Ferry, West Virginia"), changed hands a dozen times during the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War").

[![Image 15: Wikisource logo](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Wikisource-logo.svg/40px-Wikisource-logo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wikisource-logo.svg)

English [Wikisource](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikisource "Wikisource") has original text related to this article: 

**[an 1863 Copperhead editorial condemning the US Congress for accepting West Virginia as a state.](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/en:The%20Old%20Guard/Volume%201/Issue%201/A%20Traitor%20Congress%20and%20a%20Traitor%20President "s:en:The Old Guard/Volume 1/Issue 1/A Traitor Congress and a Traitor President")**

On May 13, 1862, the state legislature of the reorganized government approved the formation of the new state. An application for admission to the Union was made to Congress. On December 31, 1862, an enabling act was approved by President Lincoln, admitting West Virginia on the condition that a provision for the gradual abolition of slavery be inserted in the Constitution.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-32) The convention was reconvened on February 12, 1863, and the demand was met. The revised constitution was adopted on March 26, 1863, and on April 20, 1863, President Lincoln issued a proclamation admitting the state at the end of 60 days, on June 20, 1863. Meanwhile, officers for the new state were chosen, and Governor Pierpont moved the Restored Government to [Alexandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria,_Virginia "Alexandria, Virginia") from which he asserted jurisdiction over the counties of Virginia within the federal lines.

### Legality

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Legality")]

The constitutionality of the new state was achieved when the Unionist government of Virginia approved the division. The question of the addition of two counties came before the Supreme Court of the United States in the case of _[Virginia v. West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia\_v.\_West\_Virginia\_(1871) "Virginia v. West Virginia (1871)")_, 78 U.S. 39 (1871).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-33)[Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkeley_County,_West_Virginia "Berkeley County, West Virginia") and [Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_County,_West_Virginia "Jefferson County, West Virginia") counties lying on the Potomac east of the mountains, in 1863, with the consent of the Reorganized government of Virginia voted in favor of annexation to West Virginia. Many men absent in the Confederate army when the vote was taken refused to acknowledge the transfer upon their return. The [Virginia General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_General_Assembly "Virginia General Assembly") repealed the act of cession and in 1866 brought suit against West Virginia asking the court to declare the two counties a part of Virginia. Meanwhile, Congress on March 10, 1866, passed a joint resolution recognizing the transfer. The Supreme Court decided in favor of West Virginia, and there has been no further question.

### Civil War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Civil War")]

Virginia was a main battlefield and suffered heavily during the war but West Virginia escaped serious damage. General [George B. McClellan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_B._McClellan "George B. McClellan")'s forces gained possession of the greater part of the territory in the summer of 1861. Following Confederate General [Robert E. Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Lee "Robert E. Lee")'s defeat at [Cheat Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cheat_Mountain "Battle of Cheat Mountain") in September 1861, supremacy in western Virginia was never again seriously challenged. In 1863, General [John D. Imboden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_D._Imboden "John D. Imboden"), with 4,500 Confederate soldiers, [overran a small portion of the new state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jones%E2%80%93Imboden_Raid "Jones–Imboden Raid"), then pulled back after a month. More serious was the threat from time to time of bands of guerrillas that burned and plundered in some sections.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-34)

Estimates of the numbers of soldiers from West Virginia, both Union and Confederate, have varied widely; recent studies have placed the numbers about equal,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-35) from 22,000 to 25,000 each.

The low vote turnout for the statehood referendum was due to many factors. On June 19, 1861, the Wheeling convention enacted a bill entitled "Ordinance to Authorize the Apprehending of Suspicious Persons in Time of War" which stated that anyone who supported Richmond or the Confederacy "shall be deemed... subjects or citizens of a foreign State or power at war with the United States."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-36) Many private citizens were arrested by federal authorities at the request of Wheeling and interned in prison camps, most notably [Camp Chase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_Chase "Camp Chase") in Columbus, Ohio.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-37) Soldiers were also stationed at the polls to discourage secessionists and their supporters.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-38) In addition, a large portion of the state was secessionist,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-39) and any polls there had to be conducted under military intervention. The vote was further compromised by the presence of an undetermined number of non-resident soldier votes.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-40)

At the Constitutional Convention on December 14, 1861, the issue of slavery was raised by Rev. Gordon Battelle, an Ohio native who sought to introduce a resolution for gradual emancipation. Granville Parker, originally from Massachusetts and a member of the convention, described the scene – "I discovered on that occasion as I never had before, the mysterious and over-powering influence 'the peculiar institution' had on men otherwise sane and reliable. Why, when Mr. Battelle submitted his resolutions, a kind of tremor – a holy horror, was visible throughout the house!"[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-41) Instead of Rev. Battelle's resolution a policy of "Negro exclusion" for the new state was adopted to keep any new slaves, or freemen, from taking up residence, in the hope that this would satisfy abolitionist sentiment in Congress. When the statehood bill reached Congress, however, the lack of an emancipation clause prompted opposition from Senator [Charles Sumner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Sumner "Charles Sumner") and Senator [Benjamin Wade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Wade "Benjamin Wade") of Ohio. A compromise was reached known as the Willey Amendment which was approved by Unionist voters in the state on March 26, 1863. It called for the gradual emancipation of slaves based on age after July 4, 1863.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-42) Slavery was officially abolished by West Virginia on February 3, 1865. To note, it took the ratification of the [13th Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution") to the U.S. Constitution accomplished on December 6, 1865, to abolish slavery nationwide.

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Linsly_Institute_Building_Wheeling_WV.jpg/330px-Linsly_Institute_Building_Wheeling_WV.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Linsly_Institute_Building_Wheeling_WV.jpg)

The [Linsly Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linsly_School "Linsly School") building in [Wheeling, West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheeling,_West_Virginia "Wheeling, West Virginia") served as the state's first [capitol building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_state_capitols_in_the_United_States "List of state capitols in the United States") from statehood in 1863 until March 28, 1870, when the capitol was transferred to [Charleston, West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston,_West_Virginia "Charleston, West Virginia")

During the war and for years afterward partisan feeling ran high. Many Confederates lost property and they all lost the right to vote. In [1866](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1866_West_Virginia_Constitutional_amendment_referendum "1866 West Virginia Constitutional amendment referendum"), a state constitutional amendment disfranchising all who had given aid and comfort to the Confederacy was adopted. The addition of the [14th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution") and [15th Amendments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Fifteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution") to the United States Constitution caused a reaction, The [Democrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_United_States_Democratic_Party "History of the United States Democratic Party") rejected the penalties. They returned to power in 1870, and in 1871, the Constitutional Amendment of 1866 was abrogated. On August 22, 1872, an entirely new constitution was adopted that was favorable to the ex-Confederates.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-43)

Following the war Virginia unsuccessfully brought a case to the Supreme Court challenging the secession of [Berkeley County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkeley_County,_West_Virginia "Berkeley County, West Virginia") and [Jefferson County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_County,_West_Virginia "Jefferson County, West Virginia") to West Virginia. (Five more counties were formed later, to result in the current 55).

### Enduring disputes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Enduring disputes")]

Beginning in [Reconstruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_era_of_the_United_States "Reconstruction era of the United States"), and for several decades thereafter, the two states disputed the new state's share of the pre-war Virginia government's debt, which had mostly been incurred to finance public infrastructure improvements, such as canals, roads, and railroads under the [Virginia Board of Public Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Board_of_Public_Works "Virginia Board of Public Works"). Virginians led by former [Confederate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_of_America "Confederate States of America") General [William Mahone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Mahone "William Mahone") formed a political coalition based upon this theory, the [Readjuster Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Readjuster_Party "Readjuster Party"). Although West Virginia's first constitution provided for the assumption of a part of the Virginia debt, negotiations opened by Virginia in 1870 were fruitless, and in 1871 that state funded two-thirds of the debt and arbitrarily assigned the remainder to West Virginia. The issue was finally settled in 1915, when the [United States Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Supreme_Court "United States Supreme Court") ruled that West Virginia owed Virginia $12,393,929.50. The final installment of this sum was paid off in 1939.

Disputes about the exact location of the border in some of the northern mountain reaches between [Loudoun County, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loudoun_County,_Virginia "Loudoun County, Virginia") and [Jefferson County, West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_County,_West_Virginia "Jefferson County, West Virginia") continued well into the 20th century. In 1991, both state legislatures appropriated money for a boundary commission to look into 15 miles (24 km) of the border area.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-44)

In recent years there has been serious talk about the possibility of certain counties in the Eastern Panhandle rejoining the Commonwealth of Virginia. Frustrated by bad economic conditions and what they perceive to be neglect from the Charleston government, this movement has gained at least some momentum. In 2011, West Virginia state delegate [Larry Kump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Kump "Larry Kump") sponsored legislation to allow Morgan, Berkeley, and Jefferson counties to rejoin Virginia by popular vote.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-45)

## Industrialization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Industrialization")]

Before the 1890s small time family farms dominated the economy, with corn grown to feed animals and wheat as the main cash crop. The river system provided the main transportation routes. Mountainous areas had many small subsistence farms. There was hunting and some lumber sales but otherwise with little commercial activity.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-46)

### Railroad network

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Railroad network")]

Industrialization was led by the big railroads with heavy national funding and the goal of integrating the state with the fast growing national markets on the East Coast and Midwest. The [Baltimore and Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore_and_Ohio "Baltimore and Ohio") continued to dominate urban centers in the north. The [Chesapeake and Ohio Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chesapeake_and_Ohio_Railway "Chesapeake and Ohio Railway") arrived in 1873, which connected southern districts to eastern markets and enabled remote mines to turn a profit. By 1879 it shipped a thousand tons of coal a day. The [Norfolk and Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norfolk_and_Western "Norfolk and Western") opened up more coal mining districts.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-47) Many smaller lines were created to link remote areas to the main rail network.

#### Chesapeake and Ohio Railway

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Chesapeake and Ohio Railway")]

The completion of the [Chesapeake and Ohio Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chesapeake_and_Ohio_Railway "Chesapeake and Ohio Railway") (C&O) westerly across the state from [Richmond, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond,_Virginia "Richmond, Virginia") to the new city of [Huntington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntington,_West_Virginia "Huntington, West Virginia") on the [Ohio River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River") in 1872 opened access to the [New River Coalfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_River_Coalfield "New River Coalfield"). Within 10 years, the C&O was building tracks east from Richmond down the [Virginia Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Peninsula "Virginia Peninsula") to reach its huge [coal pier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_pier "Coal pier") at the new city of [Newport News, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_News,_Virginia "Newport News, Virginia") on the large harbor of [Hampton Roads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampton_Roads "Hampton Roads"). There, city founder [Collis P. Huntington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collis_P._Huntington "Collis P. Huntington") also developed what would become the largest shipbuilder in the world, [Newport News Shipbuilding and Drydock Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_News_Shipbuilding_and_Drydock_Company "Newport News Shipbuilding and Drydock Company"). Among its many products, the shipyard began building ocean-going ships, known as [colliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collier_(ship_type) "Collier (ship type)"), to transport coal to other eastern ports (notably in [New England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England "New England")) and overseas.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-48)

#### Norfolk and Western

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Norfolk and Western")]

In 1881 the new Philadelphia-based owners of [William Mahone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Mahone "William Mahone")'s former [Atlantic, Mississippi and Ohio Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic,_Mississippi_and_Ohio_Railroad "Atlantic, Mississippi and Ohio Railroad") (AM&O) which stretched across Virginia's southern tier from [Norfolk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norfolk,_Virginia "Norfolk, Virginia"), had sights clearly set on the Mountain State, where the owners had large land holdings. Their railroad was renamed [Norfolk and Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norfolk_and_Western "Norfolk and Western") (N&W), and a new railroad city was developed at [Roanoke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roanoke,_Virginia "Roanoke, Virginia") to handle planned expansion. After its new President [Frederick J. Kimball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_J._Kimball "Frederick J. Kimball") and a small party journeyed by horseback and saw firsthand the rich [bituminous coal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bituminous_coal "Bituminous coal") seam (which Kimball's wife named "Pocahontas"), the N&W redirected its planned westward expansion to reach it. Soon, the N&W was also shipping from its own new coal piers on Hampton Roads at [Lamberts Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamberts_Point "Lamberts Point") outside [Norfolk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norfolk,_Virginia "Norfolk, Virginia"). In 1889, in the southern part of the state, along the Norfolk and Western rail lines, the important coal center of [Bluefield, West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluefield,_West_Virginia "Bluefield, West Virginia") was founded. The "capital" of the [Pocahontas coalfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pocahontas_coalfield "Pocahontas coalfield"), this city was the largest city in the southern portion of the state for several decades.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-49)

#### Other railroads

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Other railroads")]

In the northern portion of the state and elsewhere, the older [Baltimore and Ohio Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore_and_Ohio_Railroad "Baltimore and Ohio Railroad") (B&O) and other lines also expanded to take advantage of coal opportunities as well. The B&O developed coal piers in [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore") and at several points on the [Great Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes "Great Lakes"). Other significant rail carriers of coal were the [Western Maryland Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Maryland_Railway "Western Maryland Railway") (WM), particularly notable was a latecomer, the [Virginian Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginian_Railway "Virginian Railway") (VGN), built in an extraordinary manner to the latest and highest standards and completed in 1909.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-Ronald_L._Lewis_1998-50)

### Mining

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Mining")]

The new state benefited from development of its mineral resources more than any other single economic activity after 1873. In the East, only Pennsylvania did more mining.

#### Coal

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Coal")]

In the 1850s, geologists such as British expert Dr. [David T. Ansted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_T._Ansted "David T. Ansted") (1814–1880), surveyed potential coal fields. After the war, with the new railroads came a practical method to transport large quantities of coal to expanding U.S. and export markets. The actual mining was handled by a large number of small companies, funded by loans from local small banks. These small operations were too weak to challenge the railroads which controlled the local economies, nor the labor unions which demanded higher wages.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-51)

In 1917 there were 583,000 coal miners in the U.S. Leading the way Pennsylvania had 174,000; West Virginia was second at 88,422, and Illinois third at 88,090. Wages in West Virginia mines were about 5% higher than the national average, and because of wartime inflation about 68% higher than in 1902.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-52) Employment in coal mining declined sharply from a peak of 130,000 in 1940, although output has gone up. In the 1970s, 45,000 miners worked in 1,350 mines operated by 900 separate companies. They were located in 36 of the state's 55 counties.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-55)

By 2024 there were only 10,400 underground miners still at work in West Virginia. Large scale mechanization enabled the shift from underground to surface mining, which is much safer for the workers. [Mountaintop removal mining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaintop_removal_mining "Mountaintop removal mining") (MTR) is a favorite method where the entire top of a mountain is bulldozed to access underlying coal seams by giant shovels filling huge trucks. The overburden is then placed in adjacent valleys, creating "valley fills" above ground.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-56)

#### Building the "Billion Dollar Coalfield"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Building the \"Billion Dollar Coalfield\"")]

The most remote and rugged area of the state was the mountainous region along the Kentucky border. Suddenly the geologists found Large deposits of bituminous coal, than in high demand to replace the more expensive anthracite. The population of the subregion quadrupled between 1890 and 1920; growth rates the main coal-field counties of [Logan County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logan_County,_West_Virginia "Logan County, West Virginia"), [McDowell County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDowell_County,_West_Virginia "McDowell County, West Virginia"), and [Mingo County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingo_County,_West_Virginia "Mingo County, West Virginia") were twice as high.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-57) Within this area lay the [Winding Gulf Coalfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winding_Gulf_Coalfield "Winding Gulf Coalfield"), later promoted as the "Billion Dollar Coalfield." A protégé of Dr. Ansted was [William Nelson Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_N._Page "William N. Page") (1854–1932), a civil engineer and mining manager based at [Ansted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ansted,_West_Virginia "Ansted, West Virginia") in [Fayette County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fayette_County,_West_Virginia "Fayette County, West Virginia"). Beginning in 1898, Page teamed with northern and European-based investors to take advantage of the undeveloped area. They acquired large tracts of land in the area, and Page began the [Deepwater Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deepwater_Railway "Deepwater Railway"), a [short-line railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short-line_railroad "Short-line railroad") stretching between the C&O along the [Kanawha River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanawha_River "Kanawha River") and the N&W at [Matoaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matoaka,_West_Virginia "Matoaka, West Virginia"), a distance of about 80 miles (130 km). However, two the large railroads did not appreciate the scheme and sought to discourage competition in an area they considered their own. However, Page had access to national money. One of his silent partner was millionaire industrialist [Henry Huttleston Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_H._Rogers "Henry H. Rogers"), a principal in [John D. Rockefeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_D._Rockefeller "John D. Rockefeller")'s [Standard Oil Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Oil_Trust "Standard Oil Trust") and an old hand at developing natural resources. Instead of giving up, Page and Rogers secretly planned a route to provide a new, third major railroad, all the way to new [coal pier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_pier "Coal pier") facilities at [Sewell's Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sewell's_Point "Sewell's Point") on the harbor of [Hampton Roads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampton_Roads "Hampton Roads"), fully 440 miles (710 km) away from the railhead on the [Kanawha River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanawha_River "Kanawha River"). In early 1904, they set up the [Tidewater Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidewater_Railway "Tidewater Railway"), and in 1907 they formed the [Virginian Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginian_Railway "Virginian Railway") (VGN). Building the Virginian Railway cost $40 million by the time it was completed in 1909. Well-engineered and highly efficient with all new infrastructure, it operated very profitably and came to be known as the "Richest Little Railroad in the World." Soon it and the C&O and N&W were shipping ever-increasing volumes of coal to export to Europe. The VGN and the N&W ultimately became parts of the modern [Norfolk Southern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norfolk_Southern "Norfolk Southern") system, and the VGN's well-engineered 20th-century tracks continue to offer a favorable gradient to Hampton Roads.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-60)
