The [Monongah mining disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monongah_mining_disaster "Monongah mining disaster"), on December 6, 1907, in West Virginia, was the worst coal mine explosion in American history. The official death toll stands at 362; half were Italian immigrants. Paul Rakes found many small episodes in which one or two miners lost their lives. Mine accidents were considered inevitable, and mine safety did not appreciably improve the situation because of lax enforcement. West Virginia's mines were considered so unsafe that immigration officials would not recommend them as a source of employment for immigrants, and those unskilled immigrants who did work in the coal mines were more susceptible to death or injury. When the [United States Bureau of Mines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Bureau_of_Mines "United States Bureau of Mines") was given more authority to regulate mine safety in the 1960s, safety awareness improved, and West Virginia coal mines became less dangerous.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-61)

#### Salt

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Salt")]

Much of the northern panhandle and north-central portion of the state are underlain by bedded [salt deposits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_deposit "Salt deposit") over 50 feet (15 m) thick. Salt mining had been underway since the 18th century, though that which could be easily obtained had largely played out by the time of the Civil War, when the red salt of [Kanawha County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanawha_County,_West_Virginia "Kanawha County, West Virginia") was a valued commodity of first Confederate, and later Union forces. Newer technology has since proved that West Virginia has enough salt resources to supply the nation's needs for 2,000 years. During recent years, production has been about 600,000 to 1,000,000 tons per year.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-62)

#### Timber

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Timber")]

West Virginia was heavily forested. During 1870–1920 most of the [old-growth forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old-growth_forest "Old-growth forest") was logged. Logging was supported by a dense rail network extending throughout the mountains and hollows.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-63) Small pockets of virgin forest remain at [Gaudineer Scenic Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaudineer_Scenic_Area "Gaudineer Scenic Area") and [Cathedral State Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral_State_Park "Cathedral State Park").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-Hiltz-64)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-Ronald_L._Lewis_1998-50)

### Labor and environmental issues

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Labor and environmental issues")]

As coal mining and related work became a major employment activities in the state, there was considerable labor strife as working conditions and safety issues, as well as economic ones arose. Even in the 21st century, mining safety and ecological concerns are challenging to the state whose coal continues to power electrical generating plants in many other states.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-66)

## 20th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: 20th century")]

### Progressive movement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Progressive movement")]

Like every state West Virginia had a progressive movement in the early 20th century, inspired by middle class ideals regarding opposition to corruption and support for efficiency. Progressives pushed for modernization of the state's political institutions. Administration reforms helped curb the influence of industrial tycoons on politics and society. The influence of Progressive ideals led to significant legislative changes, especially during the tenure of two Republican governors, [William Ellsworth Glasscock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Ellsworth_Glasscock "William Ellsworth Glasscock") (1909–1913) and [Henry D. Hatfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_D._Hatfield "Henry D. Hatfield") (1913–1917).[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-70) They led the way to bring the state in line with other states in terms of the volume and scope of progressive legislation. There were successful popular demands for women's suffrage, for prohibition, and for improved public schools. The state government also raised taxes and upgraded agencies with an emphasis on efficiency and expertise, including road construction, a new tuberculosis sanitarium, and the office of Commissioner of Agriculture.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-71)

### Woman suffrage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Woman suffrage")]

West Virginia suffragists worked at supporting the agendas put forward by the [National American Woman Suffrage Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_American_Woman_Suffrage_Association "National American Woman Suffrage Association"), the [National Association of Colored Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_of_Colored_Women "National Association of Colored Women") and the [Woman's Christian Temperance Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woman's_Christian_Temperance_Union "Woman's Christian Temperance Union") in the 1890s through the early part of the 20th century. According to historian Anne Wallace Effland, conservative social and religious beliefs together with the campaigns by anti-suffragists kept up a solid defense against them.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-72) The organized work by women's clubs during World War I helped convince legislators of their role in getting their women enfranchised. After a failed attempt to include woman suffrage as a state constitutional amendment in 1916, pro-suffrage Governor [John J. Cornwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_J._Cornwell "John J. Cornwell") included the ratification of the federal amendment for woman suffrage in the agenda for a special legislative session in February 1920. The [West Virginia Equal Suffrage Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia_Equal_Suffrage_Association "West Virginia Equal Suffrage Association") under the leadership of President Mrs. John L. Ruhl and WVESA Ratification Committee chair [Lenna Lowe Yost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenna_Lowe_Yost "Lenna Lowe Yost") created a "living petition" of suffragists who greeted and personally lobbied each legislator as they prepared to vote. This strategy was a success, and West Virginia became the 34th of the 36 states needed to ratify the [Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution").

### Mine wars

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Mine wars")]

Main article: [West Virginia coal wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia_coal_wars "West Virginia coal wars")

Further information: [West Virginia Mine Wars Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia_Mine_Wars_Museum "West Virginia Mine Wars Museum")

The West Virginia Mine Wars were a series of violent labor disputes from 1912 to 1921. The miners demanded the right to unionize in the [United Mine Workers of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Mine_Workers_of_America "United Mine Workers of America") for better working conditions and pay; the many small local coal companies fiercely resisted these efforts. In remote mining camps the companies exerted control over nearly all aspects of miners' lives, including the company towns where they lived, the stores where they were forced to shop using company scrip, and even the law enforcement, which was often composed of hired private guards. About 35,000 strikers were evicted and they and their families moved to new camps run by the union. Socialists brought in weapons but in September 1912 the state sent in the National Guard to disarm the miners. On May 19, 1920, a shootout in took place in [Matewan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matewan "Matewan") in the [Battle of Blair Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Blair_Mountain "Battle of Blair Mountain"). Finally in 1921 Governor [Ephraim F. Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephraim_F._Morgan "Ephraim F. Morgan") requested federal troops and [President Warren G. Harding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Warren_G._Harding "Presidency of Warren G. Harding") sent in 2500 Army soldiers. The strike was broken. The state government prosecuted several hundred of the leaders before local juries, but nearly all of them were acquitted. The federal government refused to prosecute anyone.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-76)

### Wildlife conservation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Wildlife conservation")]

Further information: [George Washington and Jefferson National Forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_and_Jefferson_National_Forests "George Washington and Jefferson National Forests")

Wildlife biologist Robert Silvester of the State Wildlife Center wrote a history of conservation in West Virginia. He explains as industry developed in the region, the people of West Virginia saw a need for wildlife conservation. The Wildlife and Fish Commission was created in 1921. The commission established the French Creek Game Farm in 1923. Various game animals and now protected birds were raised for conservation repopulating or control reasons throughout the state. Coincidentally, it was similar to an indigenous species open zoo of today and became a place of family outings visitation. The following years saw a significant growth of visitors. Buffalo were included in 1954 and attracted additional visitors. Today, the zoological facility is of 338-acre (1.37 km 2) modern [Wildlife Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia_State_Wildlife_Center "West Virginia State Wildlife Center") under the direction of the Division of Natural Resources.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-78)

### Great Depression and New Deal

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Great Depression and New Deal")]

The [Great Depression of 1929-1939](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression_in_the_United_States "Great Depression in the United States") was very harsh everywhere in the state. According to James S. Olson, Between 1929 and 1932, the state's industrial economy suffered a major collapse. Production in the state's key industries plummeted. Many mines simply closed down. Coal production fell by over 40% between 1927 and 1932, dropping from 145.1 million tons to 83.3 million tons. Similarly, petroleum output declined from 5.7 million barrels in 1928 to 3.9 million barrels by 1932.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-79) Besides industry, there were heavy losses in all other sectors, especially farming. Corn production fell from 13.9 million bushels to 11.2 million bushels. At a time people needed cheap food, potato production fell in half, dropping from 6.6 million bushels to 3.6 million bushels. Tobacco output saw the most dramatic decline, plummeting from 6.6 million pounds to only 2.1 million pounds.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-80) Not only did the volume of output go down, the price per pound also fell sharply, which meant that farmers and producers had a hard time paying off old debts with less money. Bankruptcies and mortgage foreclosures were frequent. The number of banks plunged, from 310 to 210, with deposits falling by more than a third—from $328 million to $213 million. Many small banks that had invested in real estate were insolvent and had to close permanently. The depositors could not get any funds back for months; finally they received on average about 80% of their money back. Businesses of all sorts cut back and stopped hiring. Youths and unemployed men over age 45 seldom were hired. Unemployment soared, reaching over 25% in cities and even more in mining towns. Statewide, about 45% of families were destitute and urgently needed help.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_West_Virginia#cite_note-81)

The **Battle of Point Pleasant**, also known as the **Battle of Kanawha** and the **Battle of Great Kanawha**, was the only major action of [Dunmore's War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunmore's_War "Dunmore's War"). It was fought on October 10, 1774, between the [Virginia militia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_militia "Virginia militia") and [Shawnee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawnee "Shawnee") and [Mingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingo "Mingo") warriors. Along the [Ohio River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River") near modern-day [Point Pleasant, West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia "Point Pleasant, West Virginia"), forces under the Shawnee chief [Cornstalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornstalk_(Shawnee_leader) "Cornstalk (Shawnee leader)") attacked Virginia militiamen under Colonel [Andrew Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Lewis_(soldier) "Andrew Lewis (soldier)"), hoping to halt Lewis's advance into the [Ohio Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Valley "Ohio Valley"). After a long and furious battle, Cornstalk retreated. After the battle, the Virginians, along with a second force led by [Lord Dunmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Murray,_4th_Earl_of_Dunmore "John Murray, 4th Earl of Dunmore"), the [Royal Governor of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_colonial_governors_of_Virginia "List of colonial governors of Virginia"), marched into the Ohio Valley and compelled Cornstalk to agree to a treaty, which ended the war.

## Preparations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Battle_of_Point_Pleasant&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Preparations")]

[Colonel Andrew Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonel_Andrew_Lewis "Colonel Andrew Lewis"), in command of about 1,000 men, was part of a planned two-pronged Virginian invasion of the Ohio Valley. As Lewis's force made its way down the [Kanawha River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanawha_River "Kanawha River"), guided by pioneering hunter/trapper [Matthew Arbuckle Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Arbuckle_Sr. "Matthew Arbuckle Sr."), Lewis anticipated linking up with another force commanded by John Murray, 4th Earl of Dunmore, who was marching west from [Fort Pitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Pitt_(Pennsylvania) "Fort Pitt (Pennsylvania)"), then known as Fort Dunmore. Dunmore's plan was to march into the Ohio Valley and force the Indigenous inhabitants to accept Ohio River boundary which had been negotiated with the [Haudenosaunee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haudenosaunee "Haudenosaunee") in the 1768 [Treaty of Fort Stanwix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Fort_Stanwix "Treaty of Fort Stanwix").

The Shawnee, however, had not been consulted in the treaty and many were not willing to surrender their lands south of the Ohio River without a fight. Officials of the [British Indian Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Indian_Department "British Indian Department"), led by [Sir William Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_William_Johnson "Sir William Johnson") until his death in July 1774, worked to diplomatically isolate the Shawnee from their neighbors. As a result, when the war began, the Shawnees had few allies other than the [Mingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingo "Mingo").

Cornstalk, the Shawnee leader, moved to intercept Lewis's army, hoping to prevent the Virginians from joining their forces together. Estimates of the size of Cornstalk's force have varied, but scholars[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-2) now believe Cornstalk was probably outnumbered at least two to one, having between 300 and 500 warriors. Future Shawnee leader [Blue Jacket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Jacket "Blue Jacket") most likely participated in this battle.

## Battle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Battle_of_Point_Pleasant&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Battle")]

Cornstalk's forces attacked Lewis's camp where the Kanawha River joins the [Ohio River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River"), hoping to trap him along a bluff. The battle lasted for hours and the fighting eventually became hand-to-hand. Cornstalk's voice was reportedly heard over the din of the battle, urging his warriors to "be strong." Lewis sent several companies along the Kanawha and up a nearby creek to attack the warriors from the rear, which reduced the intensity of the Shawnee offensive. Captain [George Mathews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Mathews_(Georgia) "George Mathews (Georgia)") was credited with a flanking maneuver that initiated Cornstalk's retreat.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-Herndon-3) At nightfall, the Shawnees quietly withdrew back across the Ohio. The Virginians had held their ground, and thus are considered to have won.

## Aftermath

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Battle_of_Point_Pleasant&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Aftermath")]

The Virginians lost about 75 killed and 140 wounded.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-Winning_of_the_West-5) The Shawnee's losses could not be determined, since they carried away their wounded and threw many of the dead into the river.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-6) The next morning, Colonel William Christian, who had arrived shortly after the battle, marched his men over the battlefield. They found twenty-one dead warriors in the open, and twelve more were discovered hastily covered with brush and old logs. Among those killed was Pucksinwah, the father of [Tecumseh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tecumseh "Tecumseh").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-7)

Besides scalps, the Virginians reportedly captured 40 guns, many tomahawks and some other plunder which was later sold at auction for 74[£](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GBP "GBP") 4s 6d.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-Winning_of_the_West-5)

The Battle of Point Pleasant forced [Cornstalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornstalk_(Shawnee_leader) "Cornstalk (Shawnee leader)") to make peace at the [Treaty of Camp Charlotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Camp_Charlotte "Treaty of Camp Charlotte"), ceding to Virginia the Shawnee claims to all lands south of the Ohio River (today's states of [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky "Kentucky") and [West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia "West Virginia")). The Shawnee were also obliged by the treaty to return all white captives and cease their attacks on barges of settlers traveling on the Ohio River.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-8)

Colonel John Field, an ancestor of United States Presidents [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") and [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"), was killed in the battle.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-9)

The **Battle of Point Pleasant**, also known as the **Battle of Kanawha** and the **Battle of Great Kanawha**, was the only major action of [Dunmore's War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunmore's_War "Dunmore's War"). It was fought on October 10, 1774, between the [Virginia militia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_militia "Virginia militia") and [Shawnee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawnee "Shawnee") and [Mingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingo "Mingo") warriors. Along the [Ohio River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River") near modern-day [Point Pleasant, West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia "Point Pleasant, West Virginia"), forces under the Shawnee chief [Cornstalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornstalk_(Shawnee_leader) "Cornstalk (Shawnee leader)") attacked Virginia militiamen under Colonel [Andrew Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Lewis_(soldier) "Andrew Lewis (soldier)"), hoping to halt Lewis's advance into the [Ohio Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Valley "Ohio Valley"). After a long and furious battle, Cornstalk retreated. After the battle, the Virginians, along with a second force led by [Lord Dunmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Murray,_4th_Earl_of_Dunmore "John Murray, 4th Earl of Dunmore"), the [Royal Governor of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_colonial_governors_of_Virginia "List of colonial governors of Virginia"), marched into the Ohio Valley and compelled Cornstalk to agree to a treaty, which ended the war.

## Preparations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Battle_of_Point_Pleasant&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Preparations")]

[Colonel Andrew Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonel_Andrew_Lewis "Colonel Andrew Lewis"), in command of about 1,000 men, was part of a planned two-pronged Virginian invasion of the Ohio Valley. As Lewis's force made its way down the [Kanawha River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanawha_River "Kanawha River"), guided by pioneering hunter/trapper [Matthew Arbuckle Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Arbuckle_Sr. "Matthew Arbuckle Sr."), Lewis anticipated linking up with another force commanded by John Murray, 4th Earl of Dunmore, who was marching west from [Fort Pitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Pitt_(Pennsylvania) "Fort Pitt (Pennsylvania)"), then known as Fort Dunmore. Dunmore's plan was to march into the Ohio Valley and force the Indigenous inhabitants to accept Ohio River boundary which had been negotiated with the [Haudenosaunee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haudenosaunee "Haudenosaunee") in the 1768 [Treaty of Fort Stanwix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Fort_Stanwix "Treaty of Fort Stanwix").

The Shawnee, however, had not been consulted in the treaty and many were not willing to surrender their lands south of the Ohio River without a fight. Officials of the [British Indian Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Indian_Department "British Indian Department"), led by [Sir William Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_William_Johnson "Sir William Johnson") until his death in July 1774, worked to diplomatically isolate the Shawnee from their neighbors. As a result, when the war began, the Shawnees had few allies other than the [Mingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingo "Mingo").

Cornstalk, the Shawnee leader, moved to intercept Lewis's army, hoping to prevent the Virginians from joining their forces together. Estimates of the size of Cornstalk's force have varied, but scholars[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-2) now believe Cornstalk was probably outnumbered at least two to one, having between 300 and 500 warriors. Future Shawnee leader [Blue Jacket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Jacket "Blue Jacket") most likely participated in this battle.

## Battle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Battle_of_Point_Pleasant&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Battle")]

Cornstalk's forces attacked Lewis's camp where the Kanawha River joins the [Ohio River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River"), hoping to trap him along a bluff. The battle lasted for hours and the fighting eventually became hand-to-hand. Cornstalk's voice was reportedly heard over the din of the battle, urging his warriors to "be strong." Lewis sent several companies along the Kanawha and up a nearby creek to attack the warriors from the rear, which reduced the intensity of the Shawnee offensive. Captain [George Mathews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Mathews_(Georgia) "George Mathews (Georgia)") was credited with a flanking maneuver that initiated Cornstalk's retreat.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-Herndon-3) At nightfall, the Shawnees quietly withdrew back across the Ohio. The Virginians had held their ground, and thus are considered to have won.

## Aftermath

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Battle_of_Point_Pleasant&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Aftermath")]

The Virginians lost about 75 killed and 140 wounded.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-Winning_of_the_West-5) The Shawnee's losses could not be determined, since they carried away their wounded and threw many of the dead into the river.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-6) The next morning, Colonel William Christian, who had arrived shortly after the battle, marched his men over the battlefield. They found twenty-one dead warriors in the open, and twelve more were discovered hastily covered with brush and old logs. Among those killed was Pucksinwah, the father of [Tecumseh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tecumseh "Tecumseh").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-7)

Besides scalps, the Virginians reportedly captured 40 guns, many tomahawks and some other plunder which was later sold at auction for 74[£](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GBP "GBP") 4s 6d.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-Winning_of_the_West-5)

The Battle of Point Pleasant forced [Cornstalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornstalk_(Shawnee_leader) "Cornstalk (Shawnee leader)") to make peace at the [Treaty of Camp Charlotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Camp_Charlotte "Treaty of Camp Charlotte"), ceding to Virginia the Shawnee claims to all lands south of the Ohio River (today's states of [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky "Kentucky") and [West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia "West Virginia")). The Shawnee were also obliged by the treaty to return all white captives and cease their attacks on barges of settlers traveling on the Ohio River.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-8)

Colonel John Field, an ancestor of United States Presidents [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") and [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"), was killed in the battle.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Point_Pleasant#cite_note-9)

A replica of [Fort Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Randolph_(West_Virginia) "Fort Randolph (West Virginia)"), a fort from the American Revolutionary War. The town of Point Pleasant was built on the site of the original fort, and so the rebuilt fort was located nearby.

**Point Pleasant** is a city in and the [county seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat "County seat") of [Mason County, West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mason_County,_West_Virginia "Mason County, West Virginia"), United States,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-GR6-7) at the [confluence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confluence "Confluence") of the [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River") and [Kanawha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanawha_River "Kanawha River") Rivers. The population was 4,101 at the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_Census "2020 United States Census").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-USCensusEst2020-2021-4) It is the principal city of the [Point Pleasant micropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant_micropolitan_area "Point Pleasant micropolitan area") extending into [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio "Ohio"). The town is best known for the [Mothman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mothman "Mothman"), a purported humanoid creature reportedly sighted in the area that has become a part of [West Virginia folklore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore_of_the_United_States "Folklore of the United States"), and more broadly part of [American popular culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_the_United_States "Culture of the United States").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

A Shawnee village known as Upper Shawneetown was established in this area before 1749, which the Shawnees called "Chinoudaista" or "Chinodahichetha".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-Feight-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-10)

### The Céloron Expedition (1749)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: The Céloron Expedition (1749)")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/L%27AN_1749_DV_REGNE_DE_LOVIS_XV_ROY_DE_FRANCE_-_Plaques_OHIO.png/250px-L%27AN_1749_DV_REGNE_DE_LOVIS_XV_ROY_DE_FRANCE_-_Plaques_OHIO.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:L'AN_1749_DV_REGNE_DE_LOVIS_XV_ROY_DE_FRANCE_-_Plaques_OHIO.png)

In 1749 French explorer Pierre Joseph Céloron de Blainville asserts sovereignty of France over the Ohio valley by burying a lead plaque called «of Point Pleasant».

In the second half of 1749, the French explorer [Pierre Joseph Céloron de Blainville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Joseph_C%C3%A9loron_de_Blainville "Pierre Joseph Céloron de Blainville") (1693–1759) claimed French sovereignty over the [Ohio Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Valley "Ohio Valley"), burying a lead plaque at the meeting point of the Ohio and Kanawha Rivers.

The text on the plaque is as follows:

_L'AN 1749 DV REGNE DE LOVIS XV ROY DE FRANCE, NOVS CELORON, COMMANDANT D'VN DETACHEMENT ENVOIE PAR MONSIEVR LE MIS. DE LA GALISSONIERE, COMMANDANT GENERAL DE LA NOUVELLE FRANCE POVR RETABLIR LA TRAN QUILLITE DANS QUELQUES VILLAGES SAUVAGES DE CES CANTONS, AVONS ENTERRE CETTE PLAQUE AU CONFLUENT DE L'OHIO ET DE TCHADAKOIN CE 29 JVILLET, PRES DE LA RIVIERE OYO AUTREMENT BELLE RIVIERE, POUR MONUMENT DU RENOUVELLEMENT DE POSSESSION QUE NOUS AVONS PRIS DE LA DITTE RIVIERE OYO, ET DE TOUTES CELLE~ QUI Y TOMBENT, ET DE TOUTES LES TERRES DES DEUX COTES JVSQVE AVX SOURCES DES DITTES RIVIERES AINSI QV'EN ONT JOVY OU DV JOVIR LES PRECEDENTS ROIS DE FRANCE, ET QU'ILS S'Y SONT MAINTENVS PAR LES ARMES ET PAR LES TRAIT TES, SPECIALEMENT PAR CEVX DE RISWICK D'VTRECHT ET D'AIX LA CHAPELLE._[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-11)_(In the year 1749, in the reign of King [Louis XV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis\_XV "Louis XV"), we, Celoron, commander of a detachment sent by [Commander de La Galissonière](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland-Michel\_Barrin\_de\_La\_Galissoni%C3%A8re "Roland-Michel Barrin de La Galissonière"), Commander General of [New France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_France "New France"), for the restoration of peace in various untamed villages in the region, have buried this plaque at the confluence of the Ohio and Tchadakoin [Rivers] this 29th day of July near the fine river bank, to commemorate the retaking into possession of the afore-mentioned river bank and all the surrounding lands on both river shores back to the river sources, as secured by previous kings of France, and maintained by force of arms and by treaties, specifically the Treaties of [Rijswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty\_of\_Ryswick "Treaty of Ryswick"), of [Utrecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty\_of\_Utrecht "Treaty of Utrecht") and of [Aix la Chapelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty\_of\_Aix-la-Chapelle\_(1748) "Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748)"))_
Céloron's expedition was a diplomatic failure since the local [tribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_tribes_in_Virginia "Native American tribes in Virginia") remained pro-British, and British representatives refused to leave. This incident was the prelude to conflicts between the French and [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Great_Britain "Kingdom of Great Britain") in North America that would lead to the outbreak of the [French and Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_and_Indian_War "French and Indian War") in 1754 (as part of the [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War")) that would lead to the cessation of [New France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_France "New France") to the British and the ultimate expulsion of France from most of its possessions in North America.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The expedition can nevertheless be seen in more positive terms as a geographical project since the Céloron expedition was the starting point for the first map of the [Ohio Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Valley "Ohio Valley"), which was the work of the [Jesuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuit "Jesuit")[Joseph Pierre de Bonnecamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Pierre_de_Bonnecamps "Joseph Pierre de Bonnecamps").

In 1770, Colonel [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") visited the confluence that would become Point Pleasant, then proceeded 14 miles up the "Great Kanawha" and later reported that "This Country abounds in Buffalo and Wild game of all kinds as also in all kinds of wild fowl, there being in the Bottoms a great many small grassy Ponds or Lakes which are full of Swans, Geese, and Ducks of different kinds."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-12)

### The Battle of Point Pleasant (1774)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: The Battle of Point Pleasant (1774)")]

Main article: Battle of Point Pleasant

In the Battle of Point Pleasant (October 10, 1774), fought on the future site of the town, over one thousand Virginia militiamen, led by Colonel [Andrew Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Lewis_(soldier) "Andrew Lewis (soldier)") (1720–1781), defeated a roughly equal force of an Algonquin confederation of [Shawnee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawnee "Shawnee") and [Mingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingo "Mingo") warriors led by Shawnee Chief [Cornstalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornstalk_(Shawnee_leader) "Cornstalk (Shawnee leader)") (c. 1720–1777). The event is celebrated locally as the "First Battle of the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War")", and in 1908, the [U.S. Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate "U.S. Senate") authorized the erection of a local monument to commemorate it as such. Most historians, however, regard it not as a battle of the Revolution (1775–1783) but as a part of [Lord Dunmore's War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Dunmore's_War "Lord Dunmore's War") (1774).

### Settlement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Settlement")]

"Camp Point Pleasant" was established by Col. Lewis at the time of the Battle, and the settlement that followed also took that name. Although not certain, Point Pleasant may have been permanently settled by whites as early as 1774. At about that time, a permanent stockade known as Fort Blair was erected there. Before that, hostilities between whites and Native Americans all along the [Ohio River Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River_Valley "Ohio River Valley") probably precluded the possibility of settlement in the absence of a substantial stockade.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-13) In 1776, a new fort was built on the site of the earlier fort and named for the recently deceased Virginia official [Peyton Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peyton_Randolph "Peyton Randolph") (1721–1775). [Fort Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Randolph_(West_Virginia) "Fort Randolph (West Virginia)") is best remembered as the place where Chief Cornstalk was murdered in 1777. It withstood an attack by Native Americans the following year but was abandoned in 1779.

George Washington's 1770 journey to the Ohio River Valley had been occasioned by military grants that had been awarded by proclamation in 1754 by [Governor Dinwiddie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_Dinwiddie "Governor Dinwiddie") to officers and soldiers who had served in the [French and Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_and_Indian_War "French and Indian War"). The resulting survey encompassed 52,302 acres (or 80 square miles). It was subdivided in the 1780s as follows: 9,876 acres – including the present side of Point Pleasant – to [Andrew Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Lewis_(soldier) "Andrew Lewis (soldier)"), 5,000 acres for George Muse, 5,000 acres for Peter Hogg, 8,000 acres for Andrew Stephens, another 3,000 acres for Peter Hogg, another 5,026 acres for George Muse, 3,400 acres for Andrew Waggener, 6,000 acres for John Poulson, 6,000 acres for John West. On the lower side of the Kanawha River, 13,532 acres for [Hugh Mercer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Mercer "Hugh Mercer") (see [Mercers Bottom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercers_Bottom "Mercers Bottom")) and, finally, 10,990 acres for Washington himself.

Fort Randolph was rebuilt nearby in 1785 after the renewal of hostilities between the United States government and Native Americans, but it saw little action and was eventually abandoned once again.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-14) The settlement at Point Pleasant did not receive an official charter until 1794.

### 19th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 19th century")]

Mason County was carved out of Kanawha County in 1804, and Point Pleasant was designated the county seat then. According to historian [Virgil A. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil_A._Lewis "Virgil A. Lewis"), "Point Pleasant did not flourish for many years [after the turn of the century]. There was no church for over fifty years, and society was low. There was a popular superstition that because of the fiendish murder of Cornstalk there in 1777, the place was laid under a curse for a hundred years".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-15) Lewis also relates that a visitor to Point Pleasant in 1810 observed that ...

> Point Pleasant is pleasantly situated immediately above the mouth of the Great Kanawha, on an extensive and fertile bottom of the Ohio, of which it has a fine prospect up and down that river. It is the seat of justice of Mason county Virginia, and contains about 15 or 20 families, a log courthouse, a log jail and as usual (but unfortunately) in the Virginia towns, a [pillory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillory "Pillory") and [whipping post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whipping_post "Whipping post"). Point Pleasant seems rather on the stand in point of improvement, arising, it is said, from the difficulty in establishing the land titles. It is, however, a considerable place of embarkation for those descending the Ohio from the back and western parts of Virginia. There is one merchant. Mr. William Langtry.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-16)

Point Pleasant was incorporated in 1833.

During the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), the Virginia Secession Convention of 1861, Mason County's delegate, lawyer James H. Couch (1821–1899), although an enslaver, voted against declaring secession. Mason County then sent no delegates to the Virginia House of Delegates until West Virginia's statehood, which Virginia's House of Delegates refused to recognize, thus seating James Hutcheson, who Confederate soldiers had elected in their camp. Meanwhile, William W. Newman claimed to represent Mason and nearby Jackson, Cabell, Wayne, and Wirt counties throughout the war.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-17) Mason County sent more than 1000 men to the Union army and one company of 61 men to the Confederate Army (the [37th Virginia Infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/37th_Virginia_Infantry "37th Virginia Infantry")).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-18) In March 1863, in the only wartime skirmish in Point Pleasant, during the [Jones-Imboden Raid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jones-Imboden_Raid "Jones-Imboden Raid"), the 6th Virginia Cavalry and 8th Virginia Cavalry attacked the Mason County Courthouse, where they believed munitions stored, leaving bullet holes in the walls until a replacement was built in 1954.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-19)

### 20th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 20th century")]

Point Pleasant was widely noted for the 1967 collapse of the [Silver Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Bridge "Silver Bridge"), which killed 46 people.

On October 10, 1974, Point Pleasant celebrated the 200th anniversary of the Battle of Point Pleasant. A replica of Fort Randolph was built in 1973–74 and dedicated as part of the festivities. The town of Point Pleasant was situated over the site of the fort and so the replica is located at Krodel Park, about one mile away.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-20)

### National Register of Historic Places

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: National Register of Historic Places")]

The [Eastham House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastham_House "Eastham House"), [Lewis-Capehart-Roseberry House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis-Capehart-Roseberry_House "Lewis-Capehart-Roseberry House"), and [Point Pleasant Battleground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant_Battleground "Point Pleasant Battleground") are listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places"). The central business district and surrounding residential areas are included in the [Point Pleasant Historic District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant_Historic_District_(Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia) "Point Pleasant Historic District (Point Pleasant, West Virginia)").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-nris-21)

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Climate")]

### 2020 census

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 2020 census")]

As of the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"), Point Pleasant had a population of 4,070. The median age was 44.2 years. 21.5% of residents were under the age of 18 and 24.4% of residents were 65 years of age or older. For every 100 females there were 83.7 males, and for every 100 females age 18 and over there were 76.3 males age 18 and over.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-Census2020DP-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-Census2020PL-28)

99.5% of residents lived in urban areas, while 0.5% lived in rural areas.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-Census2020DHC-29)

There were 1,912 households in Point Pleasant, of which 26.4% had children under the age of 18 living in them. Of all households, 33.6% were married-couple households, 18.3% were households with a male householder and no spouse or partner present, and 42.3% were households with a female householder and no spouse or partner present. About 41.4% of all households were made up of individuals and 22.5% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-Census2020DP-27)

There were 2,207 housing units, of which 13.4% were vacant. The homeowner vacancy rate was 3.3% and the rental vacancy rate was 9.4%.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-Census2020DP-27)

### 2010 census

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 2010 census")]

As of the [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census "Census")[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-wwwcensusgov-30) of 2010, there were 4,350 people, 2,014 households, and 1,162 families residing in the city. The [population density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_density "Population density") was 1,812.5 inhabitants per square mile (699.8/km 2). There were 2,244 housing units at an average density of 935.0 per square mile (361.0/km 2). The racial makeup of the city was 95.9% [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_(U.S._Census) "White (U.S. Census)"), 1.3% [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American_(U.S._Census) "African American (U.S. Census)"), 0.3% [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_(U.S._Census) "Native American (U.S. Census)"), 0.6% [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_(U.S._Census) "Asian (U.S. Census)"), 0.3% [Pacific Islander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(U.S._Census) "Race (U.S. Census)"), and 1.7% from two or more races. [Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_(U.S._Census) "Hispanic (U.S. Census)") or [Latino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latino_(U.S._Census) "Latino (U.S. Census)") of any race were 0.6% of the population.

There were 2,014 households, of which 25.7% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 37.9% were [married couples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage "Marriage") living together, 16.0% had a female householder with no husband present, 3.8% had a male householder with no wife present, and 42.3% were non-families. 38.5% of all households were made up of individuals, and 18.7% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 2.15 and the average family size was 2.82.

The median age in the city was 44 years. 21.5% of residents were under the age of 18; 7.8% were between the ages of 18 and 24; 21.6% were from 25 to 44; 27.4% were from 45 to 64; and 21.6% were 65 years of age or older. The gender makeup of the city was 44.9% male and 55.1% female.

### 2000 census

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 2000 census")]

As of the [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census "Census")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-GR2-5) of 2000, there were 4,637 people, 2,107 households, and 1,310 families residing in the city. The population density was 1,945.6 inhabitants per square mile (751.2/km 2). There were 2,313 housing units at an average density of 970.5 per square mile (374.7/km 2). The racial makeup of the city was 96.57% [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_(U.S._Census) "White (U.S. Census)"), 1.90% [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American_(U.S._Census) "African American (U.S. Census)"), 0.15% [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_(U.S._Census) "Native American (U.S. Census)"), 0.60% [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_(U.S._Census) "Asian (U.S. Census)"), 0.09% from [other races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(United_States_Census) "Race (United States Census)"), and 0.69% from two or more races. [Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_(U.S._Census) "Hispanic (U.S. Census)") or [Latino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latino_(U.S._Census) "Latino (U.S. Census)") of any race were 0.54% of the population.

There were 2,107 households, out of which 26.3% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 44.7% were [married couples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage "Marriage") living together, 14.4% had a female householder with no husband present, and 37.8% were non-families. 34.8% of all households were made up of individuals, and 17.8% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 2.18 and the average family size was 2.80.

In the city, the population was spread out, with 21.3% under the age of 18, 8.4% from 18 to 24, 23.7% from 25 to 44, 26.2% from 45 to 64, and 20.4% who were 65 years of age or older. The median age was 43 years. For every 100 females, there were 83.6 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 75.3 males.

The median income for a household in the city was $27,022, and the median income for a family was $33,527. Males had a median income of $31,657 versus $16,607 for females. The [per capita income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_capita_income "Per capita income") for the city was $16,692. About 22.2% of families and 24.2% of the population were below the [poverty line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poverty_line "Poverty line"), including 37.9% of those under age 18 and 13.3% of those age 65 or over.

## Folklore

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Folklore")]

### Mothman

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Mothman")]

Main article: [Mothman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mothman "Mothman")

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/Mothman_Statue_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Mothman_Statue_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mothman_Statue_(cropped).jpg)

Statue of the [Mothman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mothman "Mothman"), a legendary creature said to inhabit Point Pleasant

Paranormal enthusiasts flock to Point Pleasant in search of [Mothman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mothman "Mothman"), a creature said to be a harbinger of imminent disaster that inhabits an [abandoned TNT factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McClintic_Wildlife_Management_Area "McClintic Wildlife Management Area") from World War II. [John Keel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Keel "John Keel") published a book in 1975 entitled _[The Mothman Prophecies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mothman\_Prophecies "The Mothman Prophecies")_, and a [film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mothman_Prophecies_(film) "The Mothman Prophecies (film)") inspired by the novel was released in January 2002. Later, [another film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mothman_(2010_film) "Mothman (2010 film)"), loosely based on the legend, was also released. The town is host to a Mothman Museum, and every year, it holds a [Mothman Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mothman_Festival "Mothman Festival") that features tours, pageants, balls, films, music, and other events to celebrate what they consider "one of Point Pleasant's largest tourist attractions".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-DailyRegister-31) A 12-foot-tall metallic statue of the creature stands in Point Pleasant.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-32)

### Sheepsquatch (The White Thing)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Sheepsquatch (The White Thing)")]

The Sheepsquatch or the "White Thing" is a legendary cryptid rumored to inhabit Point Pleasant. According to local folklore, during the 1990s, women driving through the TNT area saw a creature described as being seven to eight feet tall covered in shaggy white hair with legs like a man, a face like a sheep, and horns like a ram's. Other stories include a miner who said they saw a big white grey thing, unnamed motorists who reported an animal with a long face that looked to be covered in rags, and a hunter who claimed to see an animal with horns and human hands.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-33)

## Notable people

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Notable people")]

*   Among the early settlers at Point Pleasant was Samuel B. Clemens and his wife Pamela (née Goggin), grandparents of the celebrated author [Mark Twain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Twain "Mark Twain"). They had migrated from [Campbell County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campbell_County,_Virginia "Campbell County, Virginia"), Virginia, and, according to family tradition, Samuel was killed in 1805 by a falling log at a [house raising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_raising "House raising") there.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-34)
*   Point Pleasant was the final home of [Confederate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_of_America "Confederate States of America") Brigadier-General [John McCausland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCausland "John McCausland"), the next-to-last Confederate General to die. He died at his farm at Grimm's Landing on January 23, 1927, and is buried in nearby [Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henderson,_West_Virginia "Henderson, West Virginia").
*   [Karl Probst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Probst "Karl Probst"), born in Point Pleasant, was an automotive engineer credited in 1940 with the design of the [Jeep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeep "Jeep").
*   The [Shawnee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawnee "Shawnee") Chief [Cornstalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornstalk_(Shawnee_leader) "Cornstalk (Shawnee leader)") was taken prisoner and later killed by a mob at Fort Randolph on November 10, 1777.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-35)
*   [Lee Anna Starr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Anna_Starr "Lee Anna Starr") (1853–1937), Methodist minister and suffragist, was born in Point Pleasant
*   [Ray Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Stevens_(wrestler) "Ray Stevens (wrestler)"), pro wrestler and 2021 [WWE Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WWE_Hall_of_Fame "WWE Hall of Fame") inductee

A replica of [Fort Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Randolph_(West_Virginia) "Fort Randolph (West Virginia)"), a fort from the American Revolutionary War. The town of Point Pleasant was built on the site of the original fort, and so the rebuilt fort was located nearby.

**Point Pleasant** is a city in and the [county seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat "County seat") of [Mason County, West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mason_County,_West_Virginia "Mason County, West Virginia"), United States,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-GR6-7) at the [confluence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confluence "Confluence") of the [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River") and [Kanawha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanawha_River "Kanawha River") Rivers. The population was 4,101 at the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_Census "2020 United States Census").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-USCensusEst2020-2021-4) It is the principal city of the [Point Pleasant micropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant_micropolitan_area "Point Pleasant micropolitan area") extending into [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio "Ohio"). The town is best known for the [Mothman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mothman "Mothman"), a purported humanoid creature reportedly sighted in the area that has become a part of [West Virginia folklore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore_of_the_United_States "Folklore of the United States"), and more broadly part of [American popular culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_the_United_States "Culture of the United States").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

A Shawnee village known as Upper Shawneetown was established in this area before 1749, which the Shawnees called "Chinoudaista" or "Chinodahichetha".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-Feight-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-10)

### The Céloron Expedition (1749)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: The Céloron Expedition (1749)")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/L%27AN_1749_DV_REGNE_DE_LOVIS_XV_ROY_DE_FRANCE_-_Plaques_OHIO.png/250px-L%27AN_1749_DV_REGNE_DE_LOVIS_XV_ROY_DE_FRANCE_-_Plaques_OHIO.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:L'AN_1749_DV_REGNE_DE_LOVIS_XV_ROY_DE_FRANCE_-_Plaques_OHIO.png)

In 1749 French explorer Pierre Joseph Céloron de Blainville asserts sovereignty of France over the Ohio valley by burying a lead plaque called «of Point Pleasant».

In the second half of 1749, the French explorer [Pierre Joseph Céloron de Blainville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Joseph_C%C3%A9loron_de_Blainville "Pierre Joseph Céloron de Blainville") (1693–1759) claimed French sovereignty over the [Ohio Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Valley "Ohio Valley"), burying a lead plaque at the meeting point of the Ohio and Kanawha Rivers.

The text on the plaque is as follows:

_L'AN 1749 DV REGNE DE LOVIS XV ROY DE FRANCE, NOVS CELORON, COMMANDANT D'VN DETACHEMENT ENVOIE PAR MONSIEVR LE MIS. DE LA GALISSONIERE, COMMANDANT GENERAL DE LA NOUVELLE FRANCE POVR RETABLIR LA TRAN QUILLITE DANS QUELQUES VILLAGES SAUVAGES DE CES CANTONS, AVONS ENTERRE CETTE PLAQUE AU CONFLUENT DE L'OHIO ET DE TCHADAKOIN CE 29 JVILLET, PRES DE LA RIVIERE OYO AUTREMENT BELLE RIVIERE, POUR MONUMENT DU RENOUVELLEMENT DE POSSESSION QUE NOUS AVONS PRIS DE LA DITTE RIVIERE OYO, ET DE TOUTES CELLE~ QUI Y TOMBENT, ET DE TOUTES LES TERRES DES DEUX COTES JVSQVE AVX SOURCES DES DITTES RIVIERES AINSI QV'EN ONT JOVY OU DV JOVIR LES PRECEDENTS ROIS DE FRANCE, ET QU'ILS S'Y SONT MAINTENVS PAR LES ARMES ET PAR LES TRAIT TES, SPECIALEMENT PAR CEVX DE RISWICK D'VTRECHT ET D'AIX LA CHAPELLE._[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-11)_(In the year 1749, in the reign of King [Louis XV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis\_XV "Louis XV"), we, Celoron, commander of a detachment sent by [Commander de La Galissonière](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland-Michel\_Barrin\_de\_La\_Galissoni%C3%A8re "Roland-Michel Barrin de La Galissonière"), Commander General of [New France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_France "New France"), for the restoration of peace in various untamed villages in the region, have buried this plaque at the confluence of the Ohio and Tchadakoin [Rivers] this 29th day of July near the fine river bank, to commemorate the retaking into possession of the afore-mentioned river bank and all the surrounding lands on both river shores back to the river sources, as secured by previous kings of France, and maintained by force of arms and by treaties, specifically the Treaties of [Rijswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty\_of\_Ryswick "Treaty of Ryswick"), of [Utrecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty\_of\_Utrecht "Treaty of Utrecht") and of [Aix la Chapelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty\_of\_Aix-la-Chapelle\_(1748) "Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748)"))_
Céloron's expedition was a diplomatic failure since the local [tribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_tribes_in_Virginia "Native American tribes in Virginia") remained pro-British, and British representatives refused to leave. This incident was the prelude to conflicts between the French and [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Great_Britain "Kingdom of Great Britain") in North America that would lead to the outbreak of the [French and Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_and_Indian_War "French and Indian War") in 1754 (as part of the [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War")) that would lead to the cessation of [New France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_France "New France") to the British and the ultimate expulsion of France from most of its possessions in North America.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The expedition can nevertheless be seen in more positive terms as a geographical project since the Céloron expedition was the starting point for the first map of the [Ohio Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Valley "Ohio Valley"), which was the work of the [Jesuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuit "Jesuit")[Joseph Pierre de Bonnecamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Pierre_de_Bonnecamps "Joseph Pierre de Bonnecamps").

In 1770, Colonel [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") visited the confluence that would become Point Pleasant, then proceeded 14 miles up the "Great Kanawha" and later reported that "This Country abounds in Buffalo and Wild game of all kinds as also in all kinds of wild fowl, there being in the Bottoms a great many small grassy Ponds or Lakes which are full of Swans, Geese, and Ducks of different kinds."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-12)

### The Battle of Point Pleasant (1774)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: The Battle of Point Pleasant (1774)")]

Main article: Battle of Point Pleasant

In the Battle of Point Pleasant (October 10, 1774), fought on the future site of the town, over one thousand Virginia militiamen, led by Colonel [Andrew Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Lewis_(soldier) "Andrew Lewis (soldier)") (1720–1781), defeated a roughly equal force of an Algonquin confederation of [Shawnee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawnee "Shawnee") and [Mingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingo "Mingo") warriors led by Shawnee Chief [Cornstalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornstalk_(Shawnee_leader) "Cornstalk (Shawnee leader)") (c. 1720–1777). The event is celebrated locally as the "First Battle of the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War")", and in 1908, the [U.S. Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate "U.S. Senate") authorized the erection of a local monument to commemorate it as such. Most historians, however, regard it not as a battle of the Revolution (1775–1783) but as a part of [Lord Dunmore's War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Dunmore's_War "Lord Dunmore's War") (1774).

### Settlement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Settlement")]

"Camp Point Pleasant" was established by Col. Lewis at the time of the Battle, and the settlement that followed also took that name. Although not certain, Point Pleasant may have been permanently settled by whites as early as 1774. At about that time, a permanent stockade known as Fort Blair was erected there. Before that, hostilities between whites and Native Americans all along the [Ohio River Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River_Valley "Ohio River Valley") probably precluded the possibility of settlement in the absence of a substantial stockade.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-13) In 1776, a new fort was built on the site of the earlier fort and named for the recently deceased Virginia official [Peyton Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peyton_Randolph "Peyton Randolph") (1721–1775). [Fort Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Randolph_(West_Virginia) "Fort Randolph (West Virginia)") is best remembered as the place where Chief Cornstalk was murdered in 1777. It withstood an attack by Native Americans the following year but was abandoned in 1779.

George Washington's 1770 journey to the Ohio River Valley had been occasioned by military grants that had been awarded by proclamation in 1754 by [Governor Dinwiddie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_Dinwiddie "Governor Dinwiddie") to officers and soldiers who had served in the [French and Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_and_Indian_War "French and Indian War"). The resulting survey encompassed 52,302 acres (or 80 square miles). It was subdivided in the 1780s as follows: 9,876 acres – including the present side of Point Pleasant – to [Andrew Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Lewis_(soldier) "Andrew Lewis (soldier)"), 5,000 acres for George Muse, 5,000 acres for Peter Hogg, 8,000 acres for Andrew Stephens, another 3,000 acres for Peter Hogg, another 5,026 acres for George Muse, 3,400 acres for Andrew Waggener, 6,000 acres for John Poulson, 6,000 acres for John West. On the lower side of the Kanawha River, 13,532 acres for [Hugh Mercer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Mercer "Hugh Mercer") (see [Mercers Bottom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercers_Bottom "Mercers Bottom")) and, finally, 10,990 acres for Washington himself.

Fort Randolph was rebuilt nearby in 1785 after the renewal of hostilities between the United States government and Native Americans, but it saw little action and was eventually abandoned once again.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-14) The settlement at Point Pleasant did not receive an official charter until 1794.

### 19th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 19th century")]

Mason County was carved out of Kanawha County in 1804, and Point Pleasant was designated the county seat then. According to historian [Virgil A. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil_A._Lewis "Virgil A. Lewis"), "Point Pleasant did not flourish for many years [after the turn of the century]. There was no church for over fifty years, and society was low. There was a popular superstition that because of the fiendish murder of Cornstalk there in 1777, the place was laid under a curse for a hundred years".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-15) Lewis also relates that a visitor to Point Pleasant in 1810 observed that ...

> Point Pleasant is pleasantly situated immediately above the mouth of the Great Kanawha, on an extensive and fertile bottom of the Ohio, of which it has a fine prospect up and down that river. It is the seat of justice of Mason county Virginia, and contains about 15 or 20 families, a log courthouse, a log jail and as usual (but unfortunately) in the Virginia towns, a [pillory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillory "Pillory") and [whipping post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whipping_post "Whipping post"). Point Pleasant seems rather on the stand in point of improvement, arising, it is said, from the difficulty in establishing the land titles. It is, however, a considerable place of embarkation for those descending the Ohio from the back and western parts of Virginia. There is one merchant. Mr. William Langtry.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-16)

Point Pleasant was incorporated in 1833.

During the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), the Virginia Secession Convention of 1861, Mason County's delegate, lawyer James H. Couch (1821–1899), although an enslaver, voted against declaring secession. Mason County then sent no delegates to the Virginia House of Delegates until West Virginia's statehood, which Virginia's House of Delegates refused to recognize, thus seating James Hutcheson, who Confederate soldiers had elected in their camp. Meanwhile, William W. Newman claimed to represent Mason and nearby Jackson, Cabell, Wayne, and Wirt counties throughout the war.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-17) Mason County sent more than 1000 men to the Union army and one company of 61 men to the Confederate Army (the [37th Virginia Infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/37th_Virginia_Infantry "37th Virginia Infantry")).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-18) In March 1863, in the only wartime skirmish in Point Pleasant, during the [Jones-Imboden Raid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jones-Imboden_Raid "Jones-Imboden Raid"), the 6th Virginia Cavalry and 8th Virginia Cavalry attacked the Mason County Courthouse, where they believed munitions stored, leaving bullet holes in the walls until a replacement was built in 1954.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-19)

### 20th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 20th century")]

Point Pleasant was widely noted for the 1967 collapse of the [Silver Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Bridge "Silver Bridge"), which killed 46 people.

On October 10, 1974, Point Pleasant celebrated the 200th anniversary of the Battle of Point Pleasant. A replica of Fort Randolph was built in 1973–74 and dedicated as part of the festivities. The town of Point Pleasant was situated over the site of the fort and so the replica is located at Krodel Park, about one mile away.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-20)

### National Register of Historic Places

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: National Register of Historic Places")]

The [Eastham House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastham_House "Eastham House"), [Lewis-Capehart-Roseberry House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis-Capehart-Roseberry_House "Lewis-Capehart-Roseberry House"), and [Point Pleasant Battleground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant_Battleground "Point Pleasant Battleground") are listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places"). The central business district and surrounding residential areas are included in the [Point Pleasant Historic District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant_Historic_District_(Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia) "Point Pleasant Historic District (Point Pleasant, West Virginia)").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_West_Virginia#cite_note-nris-21)
